    Her and Kara — their first photo together. And it’s somehow perfect.

    “James, this is …” Lena gawks down at the photo, her eyebrows pinched together.

    Lena recognizes it for the peace offering it is.

    “I know I didn’t have your consent when I took it, so I’m happy to delete it,” James offers. “I’d ask you at least show Kara first, but—”

    “—Absolutely not,” Lena states. “This is incredible, James. You’ve got a gift.”

    “Thank you,” James gives a bashful chuckle. “I can thank my dad for that. He, uh, gave me my first camera.”

    “He sounds like a good father,” Lena smiles softly.

    “He was.”

    “Would you ever want to do this professionally?” Lena asks, glancing back down at the unbelievable photo in her palm.

    “Be a photographer?” James asks. “I’d love to, actually. Either sports photography or photojournalism, I haven’t quite decided yet.”

    “Well, whatever you decide, I’m sure the world will be better off for it,” Lena says. “I highly suspect this won’t be the last photo of yours I see. James … would you mind sending me this?”

    “I hope not,” James chuckles. “And of course. Text it to yourself.” He gestures out at his phone in Lena’s hand, giving her full permission to use the device.

    “Thank you,” Lena says. She quickly sends the photo to her unsaved number, well aware that she’s indirectly given James a way to contact her now. It feels like progress for them both.

    James’ eyes meet hers as he takes the offered device back. “You really do love her, don’t you? … I saw it on your face, when you were looking at the photo.”

    “I-I do,” Lena admits. She draws a deep breath and tilts her chin up. “I’ve never met anyone else like her.”

    “Yeah,” James nods. “There’s only one Kara Danvers.”

    Speak of the devil …

    “Lena! James!” booms Kara’s voice from the bowels of the house. “Get in here! We’re all doing tequila shots!”

    James and Lena share a moment of laughter between them.

    “And thank god for that,” Lena shakes her head.

    “Shall we?” James asks, holding his hands out to carry the plates of food, leaving Lena free to grab the cups.

    “You know, James,” Lena accepts his offer of assistance. “Something tells me we don’t really have a choice.”

    Lena wakes up feeling like death has started to hand out free samples.

    There’s at least three knives lodged in her brain, each one sharper than the next, yet none of them are kind enough to show themselves. Her stomach might as well be filled with rocks — the sharp, inedible kind. Even her skin hurts.

    And why is it so fucking bright? She has blackout curtains for this express purpose …

    Oh, that’s why. She’s not in her bed — she’s in Kara’s.

    Kara, who’s right beside her. Lena would never complain about having Kara in bed with her, but maybe, just maybe, she could turn down her body heat a few degrees? Or up? Lena can’t really tell if she’s hot or cold right now … maybe both.

    “Kara,” Lena mumbles, forcing herself up into a sitting position. “What the fuck happened last night?”

    “Hngh,” Kara huffs, rolling over onto her back to face Lena. Her eyes are squinted so tightly, they might as well be closed. “Lena? I thought …why are we in my bed? I thought I ordered a ride-share home from Rip’s to your place?”

    “No, we walked …” Lena murmurs. “You tried to race James home, I think.”

    Kara gives her legs a little stretch. “Mm, sounds about right. I don’t remember that at all. And what happened to the ride-share I ordered?”

    “I …” Lena trails off, calling on her memory, only for it to fail her. “I don’t know. I can’t really remember. Do you?”

    “No,” Kara says. “The last thing I remember was the—”

    “—tequila shots,” Lena finishes. “Who’s fucking idea was that? You … you called us to come take them. Was it yours?”

    “No, no,” Kara quickly assures. “It was Lucy’s. But we only did one round — there wasn’t enough tequila for more. We must’ve had something else.”

    Lena gives her tongue a few experiment flicks around her mouth. It’s terribly dry and tastes of rum.

    “Rum,” Lena declares. “Jack made us all drink some of that dark rum, in the strange bottle.”

    Kara neglects to respond for a little bit, and Lena’s forced to nudge her back awake as a pulse check.

    The blonde lets out a groan, informing the world she does, in fact, still live. Lena feels that groan on a spiritual level.

    “I don’t know exactly what did us so dirty,” Kara states. “But I picked a terrible time to forget my hangover drink trick.”

    “I don’t either,” Lena decides. “But I do know one thing.”

    Kara’s head perks up from between the pillows. “What? Oh, bad idea.”

    “That I do, deeply, truly, hate your friends,” Lena moans, clutching her head. There’s an overly-loud thump as Kara falls halfway out of the bed on a mission.

    “Yeah? Well, I hate yours too,” Kara mumbles, head already in the nearest trash bin, making a noise somewhere between retching and laughter.

    Lena can’t help but give a little chuckle too, even though it just hastens her demise. 

    The two of them remain in their respective positions — Kara crumpled on the floor around the small trashcan, and Lena sitting up in bed with her head in her hand, combing through her phone as she tries to piece their evening back together. The last thing she remembers in full clarity is the photo of her and Kara from James ending up in her messages. At least she has that.

    A steady, pallid tranquility falls over the room for an indeterminable amount of time.

    And then Lena’s phone rings out loudly, a very unwelcome intrusion into their happily miserable morning. A single glance at it is all it takes for Lena’s already-tortured stomach to drop to the floor.

    “Lex?” Lena answers. “Why are you calling so early?”

    “Oh, it’s not morning, dear sister, for me or you,” Lex chuckles. “Are you hungover?”

    “Are you not for once?” Lena retorts.

    “You know what the best cure for a hangover is,” Lex says. “To just keep drinking.”

    “Thanks for the life advice,” Lena says. “I’ll keep that in mind when I want to become a raging alcoholic—”

    “—she says, ignoring her own hypocrisy,” Lex quips. “Did you not pay attention to all the binge drinking PSAs?”

    Kara lets out a little whimper from the floor.

    “Why are you calling, Lex?” Lena sighs.

    “Ah, well, straight to business then,” Lex says. “Do you have plans Saturday?”

    “Yes,” Lena replies automatically. She’ll certainly have work to do, then a girlfriend, in that order.

    “Great!” In a moment of blood-curdling contrast, Lex’s tone swings from false delight into something deep and uncompromising. “Clear them.”

    There’s no way to misconstrue it; the honeymoon has officially come to an end.

     

    the old bones

    Chapter Summary

    Lex comes to town. Lena makes a choice. Kara clears her chest.

    Chapter Notes

    So, it's been awhile. Thank you for coming back to this story with me -- and for all the patient and kind messages left during my absence. Life has gotten much busier and better than when I first started this story, and I've since found it difficult to find time to write. However, I truly love and cherish this story and want to see it completed, so I'm back to finish business. I'm hoping to get the final chapter and the epilogue finished around the winter holidays -- that's the goal at least.

    All mistakes are mine; feel free to let me know of any errors. And welcome back!

    Lex looks older than Kara expected.

    Maybe it’s just the dark bags under his eyes, or the scruffy shadow to his beard, but he looks almost twice Lena’s age. It’s a stark contrast from the first time Kara had met him, while accompanying Kal to the unbridled celebration Lex had thrown for the Meteors several months ago. Back then, his eyes had been full of rambunctious fervor and his every movement laced with a collected yet chaotic energy.

    But not now.

    Now, a haunted fatigue has made its home in his bones, and Kara suddenly has a deeper appreciation for Lena’s fears. It feels like the foreword of a cautionary tale. Even if they’re not together anymore — if they’re ever one day strangers, or even worse, enemies again — Kara would still sooner level a mountain than see the same fate befall Lena.

    “Well,” Lex grins as they approach the table, a mischievous light simmering back up into his eyes, his chaotic façade switched back on. He doesn’t bother to stand. “It’s a good thing you gave up on your vegetarian phase, Princess; this new beefcake diet seems much more satisfying.”

    Kara can’t tell if the comment is meant to be suggestive in nature or not, but her cheeks flush all the same. It’s just a little too on-point for how their most recent late-night activities were spent.

    She glances over at Lena, and phew, Kara is glad to not be on the receiving end of that glare. It could turn a lesser man to stone.

    But Lex just laughs it off with practiced ease.

    “Lex,” Lena greets him. “I had to rearrange my entire schedule for you; I’m not feeling particularly altruistic this morning. We can leave at any time.”

    “Yes, well, Luthors don’t—” Lex’s tongue catches for just the barest of a millisecond. “—decline bottomless mimosas, Lena. It would be a sin to leave.”

    Kara pulls out a chair for Lena, then for herself, admittedly enjoying the freedom of two sling-free arms, before sending Lena a watchful glance. Lena’s eyes are still angrily trained on Lex’s face, his slight hesitation not appearing to register in her restrained agitation. It’s very unlike her, and it makes Kara realize that Lena still has a bit of a blindspot for her darling older brother, whether she’s aware of it or not. 

    Lena rolls her eyes and sits down in the chair Kara’s pulled out. “Funny, I don’t remember that rule appearing in our imperious family creed.”

    “Mm,” Lex hums. “It’s a more interesting revision, we have to admit. And breakfast is the most important meal of the day, after all.”

    “I do really like breakfast,” Kara interjects, feeling the need to mediate. She can practically hear Lena’s jaw grinding at a pace sure to destroy half her teeth.

    “Kara Danvers! If you’re anything like Clark, I’m sure Lena has to keep you well-fed,” Lex chuckles, glancing from Kara back to Lena. As someone who’s got a good few years of experience intentionally pissing off Lena Luthor, Kara can instantly tell that’s exactly what her brother is trying to do (and succeeding).

    “Enough,” Lena says. “I’m well aware of what you’re doing, but could you dial down the inner asshole for two minutes?”

    “No,” Lex sucks at his teeth, holding a hand out towards Kara. “How else do you expect me to entertain myself?”

    “It’s nice to see you again, Lex,” Kara says, giving his hand a firm shake as she introduces herself for the second time.

    Their first introduction had been brief — just a quick exchange before Lex had gotten distracted by something and vanished — not that Kara really minded, she had only been there to spend time with Kal and see Diana. But it was long enough to notice how Lex looked at her cousin with something that could only be described as love in his eyes, and while Kara never quite understood how the two men were such close friends despite their almost antithetical personalities and values, it was clear Lex held Kal in a very special part of his heart.

    It’s the same way he looks at Lena.

    She wonders if Lena can see it too, or if she’s blinded to it, just like Kara had once been — to the way Kal’s heart would break before her eyes every time they said goodbye, or to the way Alex, after a long night spent soothing away Kara’s nightmares, would wear the bags under her eyes like a badge of pride the next morning.

    “The pleasure’s all mine. I’d say I’ve heard a lot about you, Kara, but I haven’t,” Lex smirks. “My dear sister here doesn’t share well.”

    “Maybe it’s more about asking,” Kara states, a slight protective edge to her voice. Brother or not, her tolerance for Lena-slander is fairly minuscule. “Taking a genuine interest in the things that make her happy seems to work well for me.”

    Apparently, that’s exactly the reaction Lex was waiting for. He breaks out into pleased laughter, clutching at his side, his chin thrown back some. Kara glances over at Lena, who just shoots her an apologetic look.

    It’s okay, Kara tries to convey, even in her confusion. I’ve got you. We’re in this together.

    “So there it is,” Lex hums as he returns to his resting state. “That steel you humbled our dearest mother with. I was worried the tale had been greatly exaggerated.”

    Ah, that makes sense. It’s a test for her, not Lena.

    “As you can see, Lex here is utterly insufferable,” Lena tells Kara. “In general, but even more so when he’s trying to prove something.”

    “I love being right,” Lex shrugs. “Who doesn’t? I’d say sue me, but if I have to deal with one more lawyer, I’ll be liable to turn into a homicidal maniac.”

    The shift in Lena’s demeanor is immediate. Her spine straightens as she leans forward with clear interest. “And how are things going?”

    “Please, Princess, don’t mix business and brunch,” Lex waves a hand, dismissing the topic. Kara notices how Lena’s knuckles turn white as they roll in on themselves, but she doesn’t have a chance to assuage the other woman in any way before they’re interrupted by a friendly voice.

    “Sorry I’m late, ladies and Luthors,” Jack Spheer all but materializes into the fourth chair at the table. “Now, I was promised bottomless mimosas?”

    Jack Spheer — a bit of a weird move to have Lena’s ex at brunch, Kara will admit — but Jack is much more than that to Lena, and Kara has nothing but trust and support for their friendship. Besides, the Luthors are a bit of an unpredictable bunch, and having an extra ally around certainly never hurts. So when Lena had asked Kara if she was alright with Jack joining them, Kara had been fully supportive; one more person that Lena feels supported by is always welcome in their orbit, by her standards.

    “Jack!” Kara greets him first, sending a big grin across the table.

    Jack fits in seamlessly on Lena’s left-hand side, guarding her where Kara can’t.

    Lena gives Jack’s forearm a welcoming squeeze. “Thanks for coming.”

    “Jacky-boy,” Lex grins. “Nice of you to join us.”

    “Of course; nice of you to pay,” Jack retorts. “Besides, this is way more fun when I’m not the guest of honor.”

    Kara doesn’t need two guesses to tell she’s the said guest of honor, even if this is a spectacle of Lex’s creation.

    “Oh, you didn’t appreciate your background check, Jacky?” Lex pouts.

    Kara’s breath catches in her chest. “Background check?”

    Lena’s hand quickly settles over Kara’s exposed forearm, anchoring both her body and mind.

    “Mm,” Jack chuckles, with just the slightest undertone of residual bitterness. “It was more your hulking bodyguard threatening to rip my balls off and feed them to me.”

    Lena’s thumb starts stroking over Kara’s skin before she even has a chance to flinch.

    “Yes, well, Finch rarely gets to freestyle, you’ll have to forgive the tactlessness,” Lex sips his mimosa. He turns to face Kara. “Don’t worry, no such threats will be levied at you.”

    “How come?” Kara rasps out, hoping it sounded braver than it felt.

    “Because,” Lex glances at his sister. “Much like Jacky over here, I’m also attached to my balls.”

    Kara opens her mouth to say something — what, she has no idea — but the melodic swoop of Lena’s voice cuts her flailing thoughts short.

    “Because Lex already approves of you,” Lena says. “Not that I need it, but it’ll make this less insufferable.”

    “It comes from a place of care, Princess,” Lex says.

    “So, wait, wait,” Kara shakes her head. “Did you guys have a background check done on me?”

    “No,” Lena quickly states. “I explicitly forbade it.”

    Relief ripples through Kara’s bones. Phew. There’s a decent chance Lex already knows a bit about her family’s past, being so close with Kal and all, but a background check just feels a bit … invasive, without regard for respect. Her past is her own to share.

    “Spoilsport,” Lex grumbles. “The blackmail was an unnecessary touch.”

    Kara can’t tell if he’s joking or not.

    “You’ll live,” Lena deadpans.

    So maybe not.

    “So, Lex,” Kara asks, shifting forward in her chair slightly. “Not that I’m ungrateful, but can I ask why you already approve? I mean, we’ve barely met …”

    “Well, not that my opinion matters, apparently,” Lex says, words very pointedly angled at his sister. “But I always thought you two would go well together. Ask Lena, I tried to send her your way at the last party I threw here.”

    Kara whips her head to look at Lena.

    “… it’s true,” Lena sighs. “I didn’t know you were Clark’s cousin at the time; I barely even knew Clark. It wasn’t until you appeared and we both made the connection.”

    “I had suggested to Lena that she might find you … aesthetically pleasing,” Lex smirks. “You’ve got a double-dose of Clark’s good looks and the personality to match.”

    Okay, okay, Kara knows that Lex Luthor is arguably a very complicated person to feel any sort of endearment towards, but … well, praise is praise.

    “So, really,” Lex’s smile widens. “You two can thank me at any time for this joyous union.”

    “Oh, they were already together,” Jack lets slip, flipping over his menu. “For like more than a month before.”

    Kara freezes, peripheral vision trained on Lena’s figure beside her.

    Both Luthors simultaneously exclaim “Jack!”, although with drastically different tones — one delight and one admonishment.

    “Sorry, love,” Jack says, mildly surprised but thriving in the chaos, “Was that news?””

    “Lena,” Lex interrupts. “Revisiting our dear friend, Mr. Spheer’s, words here — you two were together prior to my party?”

    Kara defers wholly to Lena. Lena just gives him a cool, smug close-lipped smile, chin tilted forward in her righteousness, and says, “You don’t know everything, Lex, despite your best assumptions.”

    Lex’s lips part, then shut, then open again. “I … stand corrected.”

    “A concession?” Lena teases, settling back into her chair like it’s a throne. “You must want something.”

    “Since when is it a crime to care about my baby sister?” Lex shifts in his chair. “Now, let's hear it, Kara — hopefully you’re half as bad of a liar as Clark is, if this is to be any fun.”

    Kara just glances over at Lena, awaiting guidance. She’s granted a small nod of consent.

    “Well, for starters,” Kara gives Lena a loving smile. “Lena’s the most incredible person I’ve ever met …”

    Kara continues, giving the brunch crowd an abridged (and filtered) retelling of her and Lena’s relationship — slowly getting to know each other, Lillian’s gala, the championship game. Lena adds in small details here or there, or a warning kick under the table to omit certain information. Truth be told, it does fill Kara with no small amount of pride to see the slight gleam of approval in Lex’s eyes, laced with something that almost looks like … relief.

    Their food comes and is consumed, jokes are told, and mimosas topped off. One hour stretches past two. Lex regales them with plenty of his illicit and illegal adventures, and Jack throws a few of his own into the mix. It’s a wonderful time — and it’s something Kara’s never really had. The lines of her life and her love life blurring together, mixing into one smooth, glorious gradient befitting of the richest oil painting.

    She looks over at Lena at one point. The woman has her shoulders surrendered in relief, and the dimples that Kara’s so terribly fond of have made a permanent home on her face. A bouquet of sunlight shines through the trellis over their heads.

    Life feels good.

    They do eventually start to wrap it up as it approaches afternoon closing time. Lex seems to be in no rush to leave, but Lena is more insistent they don’t overstay their welcome. She also takes the check before Lex can grab it, fills out what Kara can only guess is the tip line, then hands it over to Lex, who accepts it automatically but with a begrudging sigh entirely for Lena’s benefit.

    “Thanks for brunch, Lex,” Kara nods at him as they all rise from the table. There’s a bit more blood in her head than she expected; those mimosas had been good. 

    “This went better than I expected, I’ll admit,” Lena tells her brother. “It actually might’ve been a pleasure to see you. Are you headed up to Star City tonight?”

    Lex takes a deep breath as he buttons his jacket closed, the light in his eyes shackled back again.

    “Tonight,” Lex confirms, ”Meteors play at seven. But first …” 

    Kara can feel all the easy-going joy in the air evaporate in an instant. Lena can sense it too; she stiffens like a rod, her grip on Kara’s hand tightening like a vice. 

    Lex continues, “… I was hoping to steal you away for a bit first, Princess. We have something we need to talk about.”

    Kara gives Lena’s hand a reassuring squeeze, though it feels like an insignificant gesture in the face of Lena’s ignited anxiety.

    “About what,” Lena’s jaw clenches. Lex isn’t even afforded a question; it’s a demand.

    “Our mother,” Lex states.

    “I have plans, Lex, you can’t just spring this on me,” Lena exhales, annoyance laid clear. She looks to Kara, clearly apprehensive about parting, though Kara has a feeling it’s less about her benefit and more about Lena’s.

    “And here I thought you were sulking that I was leaving you out of things,” Lex retorts.

    “I’m good,” Kara nods, giving her a soft smile. “I know how to get home. Go do your thing.”

    “You can ride with me,” Jack offers. “William’s waiting outside in my car. We can take you wherever you need to go.”

    “That would be great! Thanks,” Kara says, nodding her acceptance. “Could you drop me off at the gym? I’m supposed to go do some shoulder rehab today.”

    “Of course,” Jack grins. “While we’re there, I wouldn’t be opposed to putting a few shots up, Danvers, if you’re good for it.”

    A new willing basketball partner? That’s also Lena’s best friend? There’s no possible way Kara would say—

    “—No,” Lena cuts them both off. “You’re still only supposed to do your rehabilitation exercises. That’s it.” 

    “I could still rebound for him; right arm only,” Kara murmurs, and the lack of a complaint sounds like a concession to Kara. “I promise I won’t push it.”

    “… Fine. Thank you, Jack,” Lena exhales. One problem resolved; a much bigger one to follow. 

    It’s Kara that pulls her hand out of Lena’s, though a piece of her heart is left behind in the act. She doesn’t want to leave Lena alone — she can feel something’s just a little wrong, like a warbled droning in her bones — but there’s no other option.

    “Kara, Jack — it’s been a delight,” Lex says, waving over at a man in the distance. Lex’s other hand settles over Lena’s shoulder, gesturing for the two of them to head in the direction of the man. Kara realizes this must be Finch, judging by the muscles practically bulging out under the man’s suit. 

    “Alright, Princess, let’s go,” Lex continues, as he begins to set them both in motion. “Finch will drive us back to the hotel.”

    Lena shoots Kara a final look goodbye over her shoulder as she walks away, eyes widened by a myriad of emotions. Kara plasters on a fake smile that does nothing for either of them.

    “It’ll be okay,” Kara promises softly, though Lena’s too far away to hear her now. She just needs to put it out into the universe.

    “Welcome to dating a Luthor,” Jack murmurs beside her, voice laced with sympathy. “It’s …”

    “Yeah,” Kara sighs, the weight of the unknown settling over her shoulders. “I know.”

    By no surprise, Lex is staying in the most lavish hotel National City has to offer. And even less surprising — the interior of his room is absolutely destroyed.

    “Wild night?” Lena asks dryly, glancing around an overturned chair. There’s a bit of red fabric peeking out from underneath it, which upon closer inspection appears to be a piece of lace, so Lena promptly ignores its existence. 

    She also ignores the empty fifth of whiskey in the trash can. And she certainly ignores the remnants of white powder on the coffee table, lest this meeting of siblings (that she’s already apprehensive over) be entirely derailed.

    “Depends on your measuring stick,” Lex waves her off. He’s already taken a seat on the floor, in front of a massive window looking out over the downtown of National City.

    “Yes, well, you’ve always been obsessed with measuring,” Lena quips. “With who, the world can only guess …”

    (They both know it’s only ever been to one man — Lionel Luthor.)

    “Your insults are getting pedestrian, Princess,” Lex says. “You’re out of practice.”

    “Well, you’ve spent a good portion of the year avoiding me,” comes Lena’s wry response as she lowers herself to the floor to sit next to her brother. “Hard to practice without a target.”

    “Fair,” Lex sighs.

    Lex wraps his arms around his legs and pulls them closer to his chest. It’s a position she’s seen in him several times over several eras — the harshly-scolded-by-Lionel era, the Father-just-died era, and the post-breakup-with-Mercy era. And now whatever this new, unknown yet hellish era is.

    It’s unsettling, to say the least.

    Illuminated by the bright sun in front of them, his mask of ‘Lex Luthor’ falls away in tatters. His eyebags look deeper and darker. The gentle wrinkle lines across his forehead seem to intensify and his shoulders slump around himself.

    He looks terrible.

    Lena tells him just that.

    “Haven’t been getting my beauty sleep,” Lex dismisses.

    “Are you sure it’s not withdrawal?” Lena challenges. The white powder on the coffee table resurfaces in her mind.

    “Fairly certain,” Lex gives her a taunting look. “That would imply stopping, no?”

    “One can hope,” Lena sighs, so visceral that her bones rattle. “If you’re trying to kill yourself, there are faster ways than liver failure.”

    “Lena, Lena, Lena,” Lex gives his head an annoying little shake. “What is life if not a constant dance with death?”

    “Poetic,” Lena deadpans. “Didn’t you fail creative writing?”

    “Semantics. Didn’t show up,” Lex says. “A habit I believe you’ve recently adopted, haven’t you?”

    Lex’s ever-expansive knowledge of Lena’s happenings is not new but always old; it’s forever been like that, but her fuse for it has become increasingly shorter. Lex’s self-imposed ownership of information that’s not his to know is infuriating.

    “Me taking Kara to the hospital for a doctor’s appointment is not the same as you skipping off to the Maldives to try every drug known to man,” Lena states.

    “Well, one might be more fun, but one has much better eye-candy,” Lex teases. “I think I might just prefer Kara to Clark. She’s easier on the eyes.”

    “Lex,” Lena tries to keep the territorial growl out of her voice, but she probably doesn’t succeed as much as she would like. “You wanted to talk. So talk.”

    “Fine. Fine. You’re getting impatient; it’s not very becoming.”

    “Neither is your constant involvement and interruption to my affairs,” Lena says. “You’ve been too busy or self-important to talk to me at all the past few weeks, and then you just expect me to drop everything so you can disrupt my life here? Why?”

    “… I’m here to talk to you about Mother,” Lex admits. “And I had significant doubts you’d be receptive to that topic.”

    He’s not wrong.

    “What’s going on with Mother?” Lena asks. “Surely something terminal, given this somber disposition of yours?”

    “One could dream,” Lex takes a deep breath, eyes rolled back, before resuming his vigil over the horizon. “She still wants to talk to you, you know,” he informs Lena. “Every time I see her, she asks about you.”

    “I don’t care. I make it my business not to consort with criminals,” Lena sneers.

    “Yes, yes, I’m sure,” Lex murmurs. “I’m just the messenger boy.”

    Lena’s curiosity gets the better of her. “So you went to see her more than once?”

    “Yes,” Lex confirms with a solemn nod. “She was furious initially, but actually a bit impressed with my coup. We’ve come to reach an … unsteady understanding.”

    “Well, you were always her golden boy,” Lena remarks. “You could do no wrong when we were little.”

    Lex scoffs, idly twisting the clunky ring on his finger. “We both know Father would say that’s not true.”

    “Why does she want to see me?” Lena asks. “She’s never exactly made an effort to have a relationship with me before.”

    Her brother knows something he’s not saying; Lena can feel it. It’s the metallic tang in the air before a thunderstorm.

    A beat of silence passes undisturbed. Lena’s heart, not so much.

    “Because—” Lex sighs. He reaches to his other side, swiping a thin manila file folder off of the floor and flourishing it out over to Lena. She never even saw him set it out. “—in the interest of ripping off the bandaid quickly — because of this.”

    “What is it?” Lena’s eyes narrow at the offending item.

    “See for yourself,” Lex says, setting it right into her hands. There’s a gravity to the motion that sends a chill down Lena’s spine as she slides a finger between the smooth paper edges and flips the folder apart.

    Nothing could have prepared Lena for the words that meet her on the page.

     

    Mother: Walsh, Elizabeth    (301402_S01)

    Child: Walsh, Lena K.   (301402_S02)

    Alleged Father: Luthor, Lionel J.    (301402_S03)

    Probability of Paternity: 99.98%

     

    Paternity?

    Luthor, Lionel J. … probability of paternity … 99.98%. For PCR results, that might as well be 110%, and Lena knows it.

    Luthor, Lionel J: her biological father.

    Which makes her Lena … Luthor, daughter of Lionel Luthor … a full-blown, true-blooded Luthor. It’s the instant deconstruction of her holiest fantasy and the confirmation of her darkest fears, all distilled down into a single, world-killing line of text.

    Her lips fall apart.

    “You can re-read it all you like,” Lex sighs. “But those numbers won’t change.”

    And just how many times did you re-read it, Lex? Lena can’t help but wonder.

    She feels as though an earthquake could strike at that very moment, and she wouldn’t sense a single tremor. She wouldn’t feel anything at all.

    “Did …” Lena’s voice fails her as her lower lip trembles. “D-did you know?”

    Lex doesn’t answer right away, instead idly staring out over the city skyline with a level of exhaustion unparalleled.

    “Lex.”

    “I … had a suspicion,” Lex admits slowly. “Did I ever tell you about the time Ignatius had to be put down?”

    “Vaguely,” Lena’s brow furrows, not sure what Lex’s dead dog has to do with the revelation of her true parentage.

    “Well, when Iggy had to be put down, I wanted to be there,” Lex explains. “He was my best friend. But Mother wouldn’t have it. She thought I was being far too sentimental, so she sent me off with Father on one of his business trips … to Ireland.”

    Ireland?

    “There was a woman there that traveled with us,” Lex says. “I wanted to hate her so badly; Father only had eyes for her that entire trip, when I needed him to actually give a fuck about me. But I found I couldn’t hate her … she was so kind to me.”

    Lena’s heart gives a painful thrum.

    “She had a beautiful smile. And she was always walking around barefoot, even out in the grass, which I thought was odd — I’d never met someone like that before,” Lex says. “And when she found out about Iggy one night, she … pulled me into her arms and started to sing to me. An old Irish s—”

    “—Gaelic.”

    “… fine, Gaelic song,” Lex continues. “And with it, she had stolen my heart. I understood why Father looked at her like she was the world. I would’ve done anything for her to be my mother by the time we left.”

    It feels like a knife to her heart that she never knew to watch for. 

    Lex knew.

    Lena swallows harshly. “Lex, why … why did you never say anything?”

    “And say what, Lena?” Lex asks. Lena’s not sure if his confession has left his conscience feeling lighter or not. He had better, because Lena sure as hell doesn’t.

    “Anything,” Lena states.

    “I never knew for certain,” Lex sighs. “It was just an educated guess—”

    “—an extremely educated guess—”

    “—and I wasn’t about to deprive you of your fantasy,” Lex explains.

    “—Fantasy?” Lena scoffs. “Says the man who told my six-year-old self that fantasy books are for children and fools, and a waste of time—” 

    “—You were always so proud that you were only a Luthor by circumstance,” Lex continues, utterly ignoring her. “You thought it kept you above the rest of our family’s sins.”

    Fire thrums in Lena’s stomach, an angry, ugly, raging beast. “You knew and you didn’t say anything,” she accuses. “Lex, you—”

    “—you knew too,” Lex cuts her off sharply, voice raising. “Don’t act holier than me, Lena. You knew too, deep down. You always have.”

    You knew. You always have.

    Lena’s mouth falls open … not in surprise, not in offense, but in grief.

    He’s right.

    She’s never wanted to admit it, never wanted to even conceive of it. Always rejected it with every fiber of her being, because it couldn’t be true, it just couldn’t …

    But Luthor or not, she can do the math in her sleep. Why would the Luthors — a family who profits off the sick and vulnerable, who treat laws like paper tape and people like pawns, who sit on a throne of privilege so high they can’t see the broken ground underneath their feet — suddenly become altruistic enough to adopt some random, orphaned four-year-old girl from Ireland?

    A no-one from another country?

    Because they wanted a daughter? No, no, Lillian always made it perfectly clear that Lena was never wanted as a Luthor. Never belonged.

    So why then? Because it could be an attempt at repentance?

    No. Luthors don’t do remorse; they never have.

    So why? Why adopt a child at random?

    … because it’s not random.

     

    Lena’s mind swirls as her entire past is upheaved in one swift motion.

    There was Lionel. 

    “You’re a Luthor, Lena, and you’ll always rise above.”

    There was Lex.

    “You’re my sister and you’ll always come first.”

    There were strangers on the sidewalk. 

    “… that little Luthor bitch.”

    There were the news articles.

    “Metropolis’ own spoiled Luthor heiress …”

    There were her irrelevant classmates.

    “Oh, that’s Lena Luthor, one of NCU’s rich bitches. You know the type.”

    There were enemies turned friends.

    “Because you’re a Luthor. You’re just like the rest of them. What you want is the only thing that matters.”

    There was even her own denial.

    “If there’s one thing Luthors are good at, it’s lying …”

    Lying to themselves most of all.

    There was only ever one … one who didn’t fit in with the rest.

    “You’re Lena Luthor … You might be rich, but you’re not a rich bitch … You are not your parents … I think you could make the world a better place, Lena.”

    Faith where there had been no reason for it to exist.

    “Lena, it’s not your fault. You couldn’t have saved your mother.”

    A kindness and empathy she had never been shown.

    “ Lena is one of the most caring, beautiful, intelligent women I’ve ever met … she makes the ‘Luthor name’ mean something positive, for once.”

    A myriad of praise and acceptance, laced with a love that suddenly feels a galaxy away.

    “I’m not going to yell at you, Lena, ever. You don’t deserve that; just like your last name doesn’t deserve you.”

    A determined insistence not to waiver from her side.

    “ I like the person you are above everything else, Lena … The Luthor name doesn’t deserve you, Lena, and I’m not going to silently reinforce that it does ... I’m proud to be with you, Lena.”

    Lena. Lena. Lena. Said with a greater softness and adoration each and every time.

    And the mantra. That accursed, recurring, persistent mantra.

    “You’re a good person, Lena.”

    But now … now, the bones before her feet have been unearthed and there is no grave deep enough to bury them again.

    You knew. You always have.

     

    “I-I did,” Lena states. The instant the words leave her mouth, her heart stops and her blood runs ice cold. 

    Lex makes a clicking noise with his tongue, reminding Lena that she’s not alone. That there’s a series of events leading up to this. And a series of events to follow.

    “Why are you telling me now?” Lena asks. There has to be a motive, there always fucking is.

    Lex still doesn’t take his eyes off the skyline. “Because I’m not the one that found that paternity test.”

    Lena’s lungs cease their movement. “Who?”

    “The lawyers did,” Lex says. “Lillian, Luthor Corp, and the feds all have a copy. It came up in some of Lillian’s subpoenaed files.”

    “Aren’t there protections for subpoenaed documents?” 

    “… yes,” Lex sighs. “Which would be helpful … but a reporter, some ‘Bethany Snow’, also got a copy. It’s accelerated my timeline considerably. I’ve got people on it; I think we can pay her off, b—”

    “—you were going to keep this from me for even longer?” Lena cuts right through. “Your timeline ?”

    “Not that much longer,” Lex backpedals, “Just a bit more until I could figure out the best way to tell you.”

    Right, sure, very believable.

    “This is why Mother wants to talk with me,” Lena realizes.

    “That would be my guess as well,” Lex concedes. “Though I have no idea how she’ll try to spin it to you.”

    Lena brings a hand up to rub at her brow, her other hand flipping the folder shut. “I hate our family, Lex.”

    “I know you do,” Lex agrees.

    Lena looks down at the folder in disbelief. This can’t be real. And yet it is, a single piece of paper sitting in her hands, far too light for the weight it carries.

    The best empires really do crumble from within, after all.

    “This is why you’ve been avoiding me?” Lena guesses.

    “Sam insisted it should be me to tell you,” Lex says. “Father should’ve told you himself, but here I am paying for his sins—”

    “—oh, how difficult for you—” Lena mocks.

    “—do you think this has been fun?” Lex’s voice begins to raise, just as he stands and begins to pace away. “Dealing with waves of officials, and lawyers, and press? Cleaning up after Mother? My entire life I’ve been compared to Father, held accountable for what our parents have done! The entire world wants me to be the Lex Luthor, and you’re angry at me for trying to delay you from suffering the same fate?!”

    “That is my fate, Lex!” Lena insists, following to her feet. “Ever since I was adopted, our lives have been the same! The difference? The difference is that I felt like an outcast my entire life — that I didn’t belong — and the entire time you knew that wasn’t true!”

    “You don’t want this life, Lena,” Lex states. “You never have. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be here right now. You would’ve graduated early, like you had so many chances to do, and you would’ve come home. You would’ve been there by my side.”

    “I’m not going to apologize for wanting to be free for the first time in my life. I’m still here Lex, and I’m trying to help,” Lena cries. “I’m trying to help you and you won’t let me. You never really have.”

    “What’s that supposed to mean?” Lex asks.

    “You make yourself into a martyr!” Lena exclaims. “You pretend like you and you alone are the only person that can handle things. You handle everything! It’s always the way you want it to be.”

    “You know what, Lena, it is!” Lex retorts. “Do you have any idea how exhausting it is to be me? To always be right? There’s no challenge to anything. It’s all too … too … easy ! … It’s too easy.”

    “But you’re not always right,” Lena says. “You think you are and you’re too self-righteous to look around and see that you can’t do it all. I get that this world is too boring and mundane for you, but you need to find a way to care about something. You try to fix everything before it breaks, you play these relentless games, you take all these drugs to keep yourself numb, because you’re afraid of being in pain — but pain is part of being human. You have to let yourself feel things, Lex.”

    “Ha — you’re so keen on feelings now? That’s rich, Lena. And newsflash, I’m not the man you think I am,” Lex says. “You’ve always put me on a pedestal, just like the rest of the world. But yours is too high to reach and I won’t embarrass myself by trying to meet it. Perhaps Kara Danvers has filled your head with a bit too much sunshine, but life isn’t full of light.”

    Anger flares like a tempest within Lena. Kara Danvers certainly has her flaws, but her endless hope and belief in people will never, ever be one of them.

    “And clearly Clark hasn’t filled you with enough,” Lena bites back. “I know Clark Kent is a great man, but I think he’s failed you. Kara makes me want to be a better person, Lex. She’s shown me there’s a better way, even if it’s uncomfortable and difficult. I know you love him but Clark hasn’t done that for you; he’s too scared of losing you to tell you when you need to do better, and it’s hurt you both.”

    “I wouldn’t talk about your future cousin-in-law like that, Princess, I imagine that’ll make future family dinners a little awkward,” Lex snaps. “And Clark understands loyalty. No one could handle this life except me, and Clark understands that. I do what I need to do without judgment.”

    “But Clark could hold you more accountable for what you do,” Lena states. “You and I know, deep down, that there are truths withheld between you two. Just like you’ve kept some between us. Because you’re afraid of someone telling you that you’re in the wrong, but Lex, that’s what you need to hear.”

    In lieu of words, a vein pops out down the center of Lex’s forehead.

    “Blind loyalty helps no one,” Lena finishes. “If that’s what you want from me, Lex, know that’s something I absolutely won’t provide anymore. I want the best for you. But I won’t be your conscience. You need to let yourself care about something. Anything, truly!”

    “I care about you!” Lex spits. “And you hate me for it. I try to make your life as painless as possible, and you constantly resent me for my involvement.”

    “I want you in my life, Lex,” Lena says. “But I don’t need you to solve my problems. I can handle those. You’ve been protecting me my entire life, but you don’t need to anymore!”

    They both freeze in the quiet of the room, standing on opposite sides. Their shouts still hang in the air like shards … eerily reminiscent of old nights at Luthor Manor.

    “You know, I remember a time before Father drank so much. Yelled so much,” Lex murmurs, staring absently at the floor. “He used to love me. Then you came, and he loved you so much more. I wanted to hate you for it, but you just … loved me. You were the only one who didn’t demand anything of me. Mother, Father, everyone — I couldn’t do enough to please them.”

    “It was never enough,” Lex continues. “So I stopped trying. The expectations demanded of me became inconsequential and irrelevant. I realized it was better to operate alone. But you still, still tried, and I … well, I felt guilty, I suppose.”

    Guilty? That’s a new one.

    “Maybe if I had cared more, then maybe you wouldn’t have to care so much. Maybe the world would have asked less of you,” Lex says. “So maybe I tried to interfere and make your life less painful, and maybe it was too much.”

    The words fall softly and quietly from Lena’s lips. “It was, Lex.”

    “When Mercy left, she called me, a, uh,” Lex chuckles, “an ‘apathetic, conceited shitfucker’. She told me to ‘care about one thing, just one thing, that wasn’t myself, my dick, or a basketball’. And she told me I needed to be there for you more — at the time, I had been too stubborn to admit she was right.”

    “I … I didn’t know you and Mercy spoke before she left,” Lena admits. “I thought she just … left. One day.”

    “I thought it would be better for you to think that,” Lex sighs. “… I’m trying now, Lena. I’m CEO of Luthor Corp. I’m trying to care about this now. I could be great. The man to lead us into tomorrow. But I have to do it alone.”

    “It doesn’t have to be that way,” Lena says.

    “Yes, it does,” Lex insists. “I never meant to hurt you in this, Lena. Truly.”

    She might just be a fool, because Lena actually believes him.

    In that moment, he looks truly defeated. Her indomitable older brother — who always won, who has all the brains and all the power — looks beyond hopeless. He looks lost.

    She finds a small forgiveness in that moment.

    “Thank you for telling me, Lex,” Lena says. “I realize you didn’t have to do this in person, but … thank you.”

    “I like the drama,” Lex admits. “It’s entertaining.”

    Lena sighs. “I know you do.”

    As the words leave her throat, all Lena can feel anymore is that she’s utterly and truly done . Done with the secrets and the lies and the games. The embrace of selfish ideologies. The erosion of humanity.

    “Don’t you?” Lex teases. “You are a Luthor, after all.”

    No, I really don’t enjoy it, Lena realizes. And I don’t want to.

    “I need to go,” Lena says instead. “Good luck, Lex. I hope this works for you. And don’t bribe that journalist — if the story goes out, let it. I’m done being ‘handled’. It’s not really anyone’s fucking business … but it is the truth. I don’t want it hidden anymore.”

    Lena smooths out the lines of her skirt and bends to grab the folder off the floor. Even though she’d like nothing more than to hurl it into the sun, she can’t quite part with it yet. Lex doesn’t move to acknowledge her self-dismissal, so Lena bites down on her lip to keep inside whatever traitorous words threaten to spill out, and she heads for the exit. 

    She expects the damning click of her heels to be the last sound to fill the room, but it’s not.

    ”Lena?” Lex calls back, right as her hand meets the door handle.

    Lena takes a deep exhale, her patience wearing impossibly thin. “… Yes, Lex?”

    “Don’t … don’t do what I did, alright?” Lex warns. “With Mercy. Don’t push Kara away. It’s my biggest regret … Luthors are better alone, but you’re still only half of one anyway.”

    Lena turns her head to look back over her shoulder in surprise. She’s never once heard her brother actually utter a single regret before; he’s always right. He’s a Luthor.

    And, apparently, so is she — half or not.

    Lex is still sitting on the floor again, his arms laced around his knees. He’s not facing her, instead gazing out over the National City skyline, looking so terribly small for one of the most powerful men in the world.

    “Maybe you should tell her that,” Lena says, expending the last drop of goodwill she has left for now. She’ll forgive her brother eventually, but it will take time. And certainly some therapy.

    “You can do better than this, Lex. Believe you can.”

    Lex doesn’t acknowledge her words but she knows he heard them.

    “Goodbye, Lex,” Lena turns her focus back forward, the manila envelope clutched in her hand. “When you decide you want my help, you know where to find me.”

    “… Goodbye, Princess.”

    They both know it’ll be the last time they’ll see each other in person for a while, tides receding into the storm.

    Lena once described Lex as a dangerous storm, and Kara would guess that’s a pretty astute descriptor. He’s certainly derailed their weekend. Kara hasn’t heard from Lena at all since they parted — other than a brief text last night confirming the latter had gotten home safe.

    Maybe it’s inadvisable, Kara can admit, as she lets herself into Lena’s apartment. But the need to know is greater than the survival instinct. The door is unlocked anyways, a little kindness from the universe.

    Kara takes a few careful steps into the apartment whilst slipping her shoes off and into their usual spot by the front door. There’s a gentle, eerie quiet throughout the space, like the silence that follows the breaking of glass.

    There’s only one light on in the entire space, in the kitchen. Nothing is out of place, except for a lone bottle of scotch, out open on the otherwise bare marble counter. Kara does a quick scan of the space.

    “Lena?”

    There’s no response, but Kara’s eye catches on the silhouette standing out on the balcony.

    The air outside is cool and crisp, but warmer than usual in a way that suggests change is coming. Lena’s leaning against and over the concrete railing, almost thick enough to sit on, with her arms crossed, a glass of amber liquid in one hand and a manila file clutched in the other. A long black cardigan is pulled protectively around her body.

    At the sound of the glass door sliding shut behind Kara, Lena shoots her a sparing glance. Only a second. Nothing more, lest Kara notice the shattered red of her eyes — but she does anyway.

    “Lena?” Kara asks softly. She takes a tentative step forward.

    “If I wanted your company tonight, I would have invited you over,” Lena informs the air. Her neck stretches gracefully forwards, a lure of lines and softness, and Kara is brave enough to take another step forward.

    “… The door was unlocked,” Kara says, her best attempt at a neutral, factual offering. 

    “And you consider that an open invitation?” Lena bites. 

    “No, I—” Kara takes a deep breath to find her patience. “I was just worried about you. Last time I saw you, you disappeared with Lex and I didn’t hear anything after. I wanted to see if you were okay.”

    “I’m fine,” Lena tells the skyscraper in the distance, then throws back the contents of the tumbler in her hand. Alcohol, and strong enough that Kara can smell it on the breeze.

    “Lena, I can see that’s not true,” Kara says. “What happened with Lex? Do you want to talk about it?”

    “No, I don’t particularly want to.”

    “Okay,” Kara accepts. “We don’t have to talk about it if you don’t want to. But it doesn’t seem like it was anything good, and I just don’t want you to feel alone. If you ask me to leave, I’ll go without a fight, but I love you Lena, and I want to show up for you when you need me.”

    “Well you’re certainly full of thoughts tonight,” Lena rolls her eyes.

    Ready to walk through the brambles to reach the roses, Kara decides to bleed first.

    “Lena, I don’t know what happened with you and Lex today,” Kara says, “But I know you and if I had to guess, it wasn’t good and it has something to do with that file in your hand—”

    An eyebrow is raised in inquisition.

    “You’re the most organized, type-A person I’ve met,” Kara explains. “And that file’s more fucked up than Alex’s old foreign language homework. And she’d use it for anything — coffee coaster, scrap paper … and that’s somehow in worse shape.”

    It’s not quite enough to reach Lena.

    “Seriously, what did you do, throw it at a wall? Make a paper airplane?” Kara continues. “Because babe, you’re a genius, but you chose a terrible shape. That’s not going to win any paper airplane competitions.”

    And that’s enough — Lena’s miserable stone mask cracks.

    “I-you're ridiculous. It’s … not a paper airplane,” Lena says, soft and defeated. “I almost wish it was.”

    While Lena stares at the file faintly blowing under her grip, Kara takes the final step needed to put them shoulder to shoulder. She can feel the chill of Lena’s shoulder against the heat of her own body. She must’ve been outside for a while.

    “What is it?” Kara asks softly. She leans against the balcony railing in a mirror of Lena’s pose, but arms open where Lena’s are crossed. “Lena.”

    “I … I’m twenty years old,” Lena whispers. “And I just learned my mother’s name for the first time in my fully-sentient lifespan.”

    Lena’s mother? Kara’s mind races to catch up, but inevitably can’t.

    “What …?” Kara asks softly. “What was it?”

    “It was Elizabeth,” Lena says, pausing to run her tongue along her teeth. “And h-our last name was Walsh … I hadn’t heard it in so long … I … the Luthors …

    “Hey, it’s okay, take your time,” Kara soothes, placing a loving hand over her forearm in comfort.

    “Yeah,” Lena brings her empty glass up to her lips, effectively shrugging off Kara’s touch in the process, before setting it back down. “When I was first adopted, the Luthors’ refused to mention my old surname. I wasn’t allowed to mention it, ever. From that moment, I was a Luthor, then and forever.”

    Kara nods.

    “I must’ve forgotten it along the way. I would get yelled at if I ever said it, so I stopped,” Lena continues. “I buried it. I memorized that I was a Luthor now. Lena Luthor. But I knew I wasn’t. I could never forget it; Lillian made sure of that. And I didn’t want to be either.”

    “But along the way … the world convinced me I was,” Lena says. “That’s all anyone saw of me, a Luthor — ‘Rich Bitch’ is a compliment, you know? But I resisted, I rebelled, I so righteously believed that I wasn’t.”

    Lena lets out a hollow laugh, and slaps the file folder into Kara’s hand.

    “But I am.”

    The inner contents of the file are immediately enlightening into Lena’s current emotional state. Kara re-reads it three times, just to make sure she’s got it right, then gently closes the folder shut.

    “Oh,” Kara says. “That’s … news.”

    “Indeed,” Lena says, looking about six feet deep in her self-hatred. “Lex gives the worst gifts.”

    “Lena …” Kara says slowly, ignoring the impulse control in her head. “How important is this piece of paper? Like the paper part — obviously the words are important and we should talk about it, but—

    “It’s not, I have it digitized,” Lena says.

    “Great!” Kara promptly slips the paper out of the folder, crumples it into a tight ball, and pops it in her mouth.

    “Kara!” Lena exclaims, eyes wide in absolute disbelief. “Did you just try to eat that?” The next sound out of her mouth defies possibility — she laughs.

    It’s basically bare bones, but bones always have to come first.

    “Mhph I dhp nhd hts whmt ghmd,” Kara spits the wet paper ball out with a perceptible grimace into her hand. “Oh, that did not taste good.”

    “I would imagine not,” Lena’s eyebrows have yet to drop from the crown of her forehead. “Why did you do that?”

    “You do like to joke that I'll eat anything,” Kara teases, giving her a soft smile before shifting into a gentle soberness. “I wanted to make you laugh. It’s the first step to healing.”

    Lena gives her a look of faux-annoyance, with a healthy bit of skepticism thrown in.

    “No, really, it does!” Kara insists. “When my was little, whenever I got a cut or a scrape — and I did a lot, I’m me —”

    Lena hums in sympathy, probably less for Kara and more for everyone else that was in the vicinity at the time.

    “—but when I got a cut, my dad would clean it,” Kara continues. “And that cleaner stuff would burn, you know. So he told me to laugh; laugh while it hurt, and it would hurt less. And I swear it did.”

    Kara takes a deep breath and sets the wet ball of paper in the space between Lena’s hands on the balcony edge.

    “… I didn’t laugh for a while after I lost my parents,'' Kara admits. “It took a very long time. But one night, at the Danvers’ house, Jeremiah and I were up late. He accidentally burned his hand making popcorn, and so I reached into the freezer to get him some ice. But I accidentally grabbed one of Eliza’s lemon juice cubes she uses for cooking.”

    A look of pain falls over Lena’s face.

    “Oh, yeah, he screamed like a little baby when I put the cube of lemon on his hand,” Kara chuckles. “And I instinctively flinched and burned my arm on the same exact part of the popcorn pot. So he did the first thing he could think of, right? Get something cold — he reached into the freezer to grab an ice cube — and made the same exact mistake I did.” 

    “Oh, no.”

    “Yep, yep,” Kara laughs. “So then the both of us were just hollering and laughing and crying in the kitchen, clutching our burns. And it hurt so bad … but it felt so good to laugh again, stretching something deep inside me that I thought I lost. I was still giggling long after he had run my hand under cold water and gotten a real ice cube. Feeling the pain go away for a second, it made me realize how much pain I was actually in after losing everything, but … it also made me realize that I wanted to feel good again. It made me want to try to heal.”

    “Well then,” Lena sighs. “You were successful, albeit nominally.”

    “I’ll take it. Gotta start somewhere,” Kara gives Lena’s shoulder a little loving nudge. “So where do you want to start?”

    Lena scoffs. “Where to start? How could I possibly begin?”

    “Well, how do you feel, Lena?” Kara keeps her voice steady and patient, understanding there’s a chance she could get bit for even asking. 

    “How I feel? How do I feel?!  Like I’ve been lied to my—” Lena chokes for a second. “Lied to my entire life.”

    Kara waits.

    “I’m furious, I’m — I’m — how could she do this to us!?”

    She?

    “… she?” Kara asks, trying very not to sound too surprised.

    “My mother,” Lena cries, tapping a tight fist against the concrete. “She slept with a married man! Lionel Luthor of all people — it’s not like she wouldn’t have known who he was! And then what? Did she tell him when she got pregnant? Did he know, before she died? Did she love him? Did he love h—”

    Kara waits still.

    “… If she had me with someone else, maybe it wouldn't have just been her and I alone at the lake that day,” Lena continues. “There could have been someone else there to save her, my fucking father could have been there, and she would still be here!”

    “Lena …”

    “My mother, a woman who my entire life I thought was a saint, had a child with a married man. Lionel had a wife and child … and all of them knew. All of them lied to me.” 

    A tear runs down Lena’s cheek.

    “Lex knew?” Kara asks.

    “He ‘suspected’,” Lena says. “Which means he figured it out and didn’t want to share.”

    “Did he say why?” Kara asks.

    “He wanted to protect me, I think,” Lena exhales. “But I think he also saw it as inconsequential. It had no bearing on his life.”

    “That’s … a lot,” Kara says. “How are you feeling about it?”

    “Lex is self-centered, childish, and apathetic towards 99% of the world around him,” Lena rants. “I cannot stand his undue influence in my life, and I despise the games he plays. I feel like nothing but a toy, albeit his favorite one. But … I pity him too. I think he’s bored and miserable, Kara, and he’s lonely.”

    Kara lets out an inquisitive hum.

    “He insists on being alone, not accepting help from anyone,” Lena says. “He’s based his entire life off the opinions and expectations of other people … and I guess to an extent, I have too.”

    “I disagree,” Kara says. “I think you’ve been working really hard to be true to yourself and it shows. You’re your own person, Lena — you always have been — but it’s impossible to miss now.” 

    “Thank you,” Lena says softly. “And for as much as I can sympathize with him, I’m still so … so … hurt.”

    “I think you can be all of those things,” Kara says.

    “And Lionel …” Lena sniffles and wipes at her eyes. To afford her a moment of privacy, Kara looks up at the stars; only a select few shine through the light of the city, an empty shadow of what Kara knows them to be. 

    “You’re disappointed in him?” Kara guesses.

    Lena gives a hollow laugh. “I’ve been disappointed in the man for years. I watched him turn into a clever man and a caring father to a shell of himself, filled with nothing but alcohol and vitriol. He withered away in his own rage, too afraid of what others would think if he did what was best for him.”

    Something faint stirs deep in Kara’s stomach.

    “It’s interesting, really, how hesitant the world is to hold a dead man accountable for his actions,” Lena muses. “You’d think the blood on his hands would be enough, but …”

    “It’s not …” Kara agrees in somber solidarity.

    “Kara,” Lena starts suddenly. “Why … what makes you think I’m a good person?

    “—L—!”

    “—not that I’m disagreeing or agreeing,” Lena quickly corrects, “But what makes a good person to you? What makes one good ?”

    “Oh,” Kara pauses for a second. “It’s kinda hard to quantify. I guess if I had to describe it, it’s like what I said on Rip’s roof — that you try to be good. It’s not easy to do the right thing, to make the right choice, but you still try to. You help people where you can.”

    “I could do more,” Lena says.

    “We can all do more,” Kara replies. “It’s good to have something to work towards tomorrow, then the next day, then the next. Continual growth and all that.”

    “Mmm,” Lena hums. “Why are you still here, Kara?”

    The fuck? There’s nowhere else Kara would be.

    “Because I love you Lena,” Kara starts. “You—”

    “—should have specified,” Lena says. “I meant at NCU. What are you working towards here?”

    Kara tilts her head slightly. “What do you mean?”

    “You could still declare for the draft, there’s several days left,” Lena says. “Alex is graduating … Clark told me that Alex is who convinced you to stay in school these past few years.”

    Oh.

    “What's left for you here?” Lena asks. “... Why stay another year?”

    “I could ask you the same—”

    “—but you already know my answer,” Lena states. “I’m here to be free from my family, to be my own person. But I don’t know why you are.”

    “Well, my friends and my very hot, incredible girlfriend are here, for starters,” Kara says. “Also, National City has the best potstickers, so …” Kara gestures down at her feet, planted firmly within the boundaries of the aforementioned National City.

    “That’s enough to keep you from your dream of ‘going pro’?” Lena asks. “Potstickers?”

    “No,” Kara admits softly. “No, I …”

    Lena’s soft viridian eyes meet Kara’s, and it feels like home, so Kara decides to let go of a too-old secret.

    “I made a promise,” Kara admits.

    “To stay?” Lena asks. “To who?”

    “Kal and Eliza,” Kara says. “But … it’s not really for them. It’s for my parents.”

    “How so?”

    “My parents always wanted me to graduate from college. I really didn’t want to at first, but as I grew up, I kinda started to understand where they were coming from. They just wanted me to have a good future, in their own way, ” Kara stumbles and falls trying to find the right words. “… but my parents, they weren’t … good people. I didn’t want to take advice from them, I guess. I think Kal suspected that was the case, so he framed it as a promise to him and Eliza instead, to graduate. I didn’t want to, but … I think I maybe did want to at the same time.”

    “Your family is more like mine than I realized,” Lena muses.

    “Bad?”

    “Complicated.”

    Kara tilts her head to the side. “Yeah, complicated fits.”

    “Do tell,” Lena invites. “You understand me more than anyone I’ve met. I want to understand you too.”

    “Yeah … yeah, okay,” Kara draws a deep breath. “After my parents died, and some time passed, I found out a few things about them. Even though we disagreed about a basketball career, they were still my heroes. I loved them. But the stuff I learned … I don’t know, it just left me wondering … I guess I don’t know how to feel about them anymore.”

    “Wondering what?” Lena asks.

    “If I should still love them as much as I did,” Kara murmurs.

    “Do you want to talk about it?” Lena asks softly. “About what you found out?”

    “I have some in therapy,” Kara says. “But never like … this, out in the wild.”

    “Well, no matter what you say, it doesn’t change how I see you,” Lena says. “You’re your own person, after all.” She gives Kara’s shoulder a very gentle nudge, certainly softened to prevent any chance of reinjury, and it strikes Kara just how thoughtful Lena is.

    She’s safe with Lena.

    Kara takes a deep inhale. “When I was in high school, I went looking for trouble. I missed my mom so much and I just wanted to be with her again, even for a moment. Everything … everything was destroyed in the fire, so I don’t have much left of them.”

    Kara wraps her hand around the pendant of her dad’s necklace. “Just this and a few photos … anyway, I looked up some of my mom’s old court cases from when she was a judge, thinking maybe that would make me feel closer to her. But I wish I hadn’t.”

    Lena inhales, shaky enough Kara can hear it.

    “A lot of her cases, her verdicts, they didn’t seem right,” Kara says. “How could they be? Look at the system she worked in. The laws she enforced only protect certain people — the people who wrote them! How is that justice? She sent good people to prison just because they didn’t have the same support and resources others do. People who were more products of their circumstances than who they truthfully were. People just trying to survive. She only helped and protected the people she or society had deemed worthy enough.”

    “You’re mad at her?” Lena guesses.

    “Yeah, I-I’m …” Kara lets out a deep exhale. “I’m really just hurt. She always taught me to do the right thing, to be honest and just and kind. But she betrayed that herself; she didn’t do the same.”

    “Perhaps she wanted you to be better than she was?” Lena suggests.

    “But she could’ve been better herself! Wanting me to be better than her doesn’t change the fact that she could’ve chosen to be better too!” Kara takes a moment to drop her voice back down. “And my dad? I wish he had been better …”

    “I told you he was an astrophysicist,” Kara continues, “But his research … I didn’t find out until after he died. He studied the physics of supernovas … to try and use the same principles to make bombs. Kelex told me after he left the same company my dad used to work for; they worked for advanced weapons developers.”

    Now it’s Lena’s turn to not say anything.

    “He told me — when I fought with them about playing in the pros — that it wouldn’t be a good life for me. That I needed to ‘ensure my future was more protected’ or something like that. It’s a little painfully ironic, seeing as how he used his skills to potentially end other peoples’ futures.”

    “Is it possible he didn’t know what his research would be used for?” Lena asks.

    “I asked Kelex the same thing,” Kara says. “And in his usual blunt manner, he told me my dad definitely knew. He only cared about protecting the people he cared about.”

    “I … do understand the impulse,” Lena admits. “We want to ensure those we love will always be alright. That their lives are as … painless as possible, I suppose.”

    “I get why he did it,” Kara sighs. “I just … where will the world be if we only care about the people we love? What happens to the rest? What about the people other people love? The people who don’t know they’re loved?”

    Several breaths fill the silence before it ends.

    “That’s why you don’t talk about your parents, isn’t it?” Lena asks.

    Kara makes a confirmatory grunt, but it’s twisted into a whimper before it escapes her throat. “I … it wasn’t always like that at first. Talking about them was too hard, too raw. Then no one talked about them. Kal tried a little, but he’s not amazing at everything. I started to wonder if I was the only one that missed them. And when I got old enough, and started to find out who they were when they weren’t my parents, I … how could I talk about them?”

    Kara snatches a desperate gulp of air. “What am I supposed to feel? Do I love them less for their flaws, or do I love them more in spite of it?”

    “I don’t know,” Lena says, turning Kara by the shoulders to face her. “I’m not exactly the model for healthy family dynamics, but I do know one thing.”

    “What?”

    “That you’re as arrogant as you are confident,” Lena states. “As foolish as you are humorous. And as idiotic as you are clever.”

    “Hey, wh—“

    “—Let me finish. You, Kara Danvers,” Lena pulls them closer so there’s nowhere to look but at the other. “You are your strengths and your faults. I love you for everything you are. The same characteristics that may annoy me from time to time — they’re also what I love about you. I can’t pick and choose only your good qualities. I love you for all of them.”

    Something the size of a basketball swells at the base of Kara’s throat as Lena’s lips meet hers.

    “I love you too,” Kara murmurs as they part. Lena’s hand lingers on her forearm. “Thank you.”

    “You don’t need to thank me, darling,” Lena says. “But can I ask something of you?”

    “Anything.”

    “Talk about your parents more,” Lena requests. “I like it when you do, regardless of the implications of their moral statuses. I think it’s good for you.”

    “I don’t know if I can do that, Lena,” Kara swallows roughly.

    “Just think about it.”

    A beat of silence passes between them.

    “It’ll be in the news soon,” Lena announces. “That Lionel’s my biological father.”

    “What?” Kara’s forehead crinkles deeply.

    “The paternity test got leaked and some reporter got their hands on it,” Lena says. “I told Lex not to bribe or threaten the story away.”

    “Why?” Kara says. “But that’s your private life, Lena. I can see if Lois can—”

    “—no,” Lena shakes her head. “Thank you, but I don’t want this ‘handled’. It’s the truth. I don’t want to be the type of Luthor that’s afraid of it.”

    Kara stammers. “But everyone will know your mom …”

    “Slept with Lionel Luthor?” Lena says. “I imagine they will, yes. My mother and Lionel both did something hurtful, but I refuse to label her solely as ‘bad’ for it. She exists in the duality of the moral and immoral things she’s done. That’s something my therapist emphasized last session; you can feel more than one thing. I can resent her for the situation she put us in, but I … I can still love her for everything else.”

    “Your therapist?” Kara asks. “Did you talk to them about this?”

    “Not since Lex’s announcement,” Lena replies. “But I’ve got an appointment this week. Should be eventful.”

    Kara chuckles softly. “Yeah, I bet.”

    “I still love my mother,” Lena states. “I might be furious and wounded right now, but I wouldn’t want to bury her in memory. I already buried her once. You buried your parents too, and that hurts , I know. But have you considered if you talk about them more, maybe it’ll hurt less?”

    Kara’s brain shorts out for a moment. New ideas tend to do that.

    “… I … I guess I haven’t thought about it that way,” she admits.

    “Even though I’m pissed at her, and hurt, I’ll never want to stop talking about my mother,” Lena says. “If I stop talking about her, everything about her goes … the flaws, but the best parts of her too. Just consider it.”

    Kara tucks her chin down a fraction, reveling in the soothing presence of Lena’s proximity. “Yeah, I … maybe it could be good.”

    “That’s all I ask,” Lena says. “You’ve helped me become a far better person, Kara. I want to do the same.”

    “Do you … do you think you’ll ever forgive them?” Kara asks softly. “Your mom and Lionel, and Lex?”

    “Eventually,” Lena states. “When it’s what I need to do for my best interest.”

    “You’re … you sound so sure,” Kara murmurs. “But how do you know?”

    “I don’t,” Lena sighs. “I think I just feel it.”

    Kara cracks a small smirk. “Those feelings really getcha now, huh?”

    “Enough, Danvers, don’t gloat,” Lena rolls her eyes as she wraps her arms around Kara’s waist. “Take it easy on a girl.”

    Kara smiles and presses a kiss to Lena’s temple. “So, what now? What do you need?”

    “Sleep,” Lena states. “And I suppose a shower wouldn’t hurt either.”

    “Oh, I could use a shower!” Light floods back into Kara’s voice — and sure, maybe it’s partially excitement because she really does enjoy Lena’s lavish shower setup — but it’s mostly because of Lena herself. “Want a buddy?”

    “Of course,” Lena chuckles.

    “Great! I have a promise to make good on, after all,” Kara says.

    Lena can’t remember the last time someone helped her bathe. She didn’t think anything of it — until now.

    There are no words, truly … but the closest possible descriptor would be that it’s like standing in the sunlight on a cold day.

    The water is perfectly warm as it runs down every curve of Lena’s body. Kara’s fingers comb through her hair, gently scratching at her scalp, and Lena wonders if bones can melt. There’s a solace that comes from Kara’s company, just the two of them with only stone and water around.

    “Feels nice, right?” Kara murmurs into Lena’s ear, sending a chill down her spine. “Thank you for letting me do this.”

    “I should be thanking you, I suppose,” Lena murmurs. “This feels divine.”

    “I thought you might like it,” Kara’s mouth lifts into a soft smile as she meticulously runs the loofa over Lena’s skin. “I know I do.”

    “Are you referring to being bathed or bathing me, darling?”

    Kara grins up at Lena. “Both.”

    Kara takes advantage of the friction-relief provided by the soap to start digging at a knot in Lena’s shoulder, and Lena’s running theory that Kara Danvers’ hands were blessed by the gods only grows more substantial.

    “Mmm … if you keep that up, I’ll get addicted to this,” Lena moans.

    “I wouldn’t mind,” Kara says. “How about I do this again tomorrow? That way, no matter what happens tomorrow, you have something to look forward to.”

    Tomorrow. A premise that should send a pang of dread through Lena, but in her newfound peace, it really only feels like weary apprehension. Let the world say what it wants about her family — Lena will show it a new type of Luthor.

    “It’s a deal, Danvers. Tomorrow then.”

    brave

    Chapter Summary

    Life in National City goes on. The semester comes to it's end.

    Chapter Notes

    Well … it's always hard to end good things. This story has been such a wonderful sandbox for me to play in that I had a hard time figuring out how to say goodbye to it. Once I did, I needed to take some time to figure out how to write again, and rediscover the voices of these characters. I'm pleased to say the final chapter is fully written, I just need a bit of time to edit and format it. Kara and Lena's story is almost complete.

    I'm aiming to post the final chapter by next Friday. Stay tuned and enjoy!

    “You look nervous.”

    “I’m not nervous,” Lena protests.

    “Really?”

    “... Yes.”

    “Lena,” Kara tilts her head down slightly to intensify the angle of her gaze. “You’re nervous. It’s okay, there’s nothing wrong with that.”

    Lena returns the eye contact with a wave of heated green, her tongue shifting along the line of her teeth. “No, I—” Lena lets out a huff of frustration. “Fine, I’m nervous. Look, I’ve never done this before.”

    “Ha! I knew it,” Kara’s face twists into a triumphant expression. “I knew it!”

    “If you’re going to gloat, I can leave,” Lena narrows her eyes at Kara. It’s a threat that she looks ready to follow through on, and Kara can’t have that.

    “No-no-no-no,” Kara quickly assures. “I’m done. I’ll behave, I promise.”

    “You had better,” Lena bites, but it’s too blunted by anxiety to have any real force.

    Kara grabs Lena’s shoulders, fully enjoying the freedom of being able to use two arms again (even if one’s now a little smaller than the other). “Look, it’s going to be okay,” she soothes. “I wouldn’t bring you here if I didn’t think it would be fun for you.”

    “Yes, but …” Lena sighs through her nose. “A karaoke bar, Kara?”

    “Just give it a chance,” Kara pleads. “I think you’ll like it more than you think you will.”

    Lena arches a defiant brow.

    “Please?” Kara pouts. It's never failed her before. “This is all going to be okay — better than okay; it’s going to be great!”

    “Fine,” Lena exhales, recollecting herself with her next breath. “I’m sure I’ve been through worse.”

    “You don’t mean that,” Kara shakes her head. “You're just grumpy and nervous.”

    Kara knows she’s right, and so does Lena, by the adorable glare that’s sent Kara’s way.

    “Hey, I promise no one will make you sing,” Kara smiles. “Does that help?”

    “... It does, actually,” Lena admits. She gives her neck a languid roll.

    “And …!” Kara exclaims. “And, there’s been nothing in the news about your family yet. I think we should enjoy this peace and quiet …”

    “... While it lasts?” Lena sighs. “Fine. You’re right. Fine.”

    “That’s settled then,” Kara holds out her hand for Lena to take, and she does, fingers lacing tight in desperation. Kara gives their hands a squeeze. “Let’s do it, you and me, Luthor?”

    “Very well, Danvers,” Lena bites her lower lip. “Let’s get this over with.”

    They’re able to pass by the bouncer with ease. As it turns out, he happens to follow basketball religiously, and the Comets are naturally on the list. It’s not Kara’s fault that they have quite the local following. But judging from the look on Lena’s face, Kara has indulged the bouncer in conversation about the minutiae of zone defense for a little too long.

    “Nice meeting you!” Kara smiles and nods at him, then lets herself be pulled away by her girlfriend.  Lena’s shoulders relax the instant they cross the threshold into the bar. 

    Lena looks back at Kara and rolls her eyes. “Don’t. Do not. Wipe that smug grin off your face.”

    “What?” Kara positively beams, all humility dropped now that it’s just Lena within earshot. “It’s not my fault the people of National City have great taste in sports. The people love me.”

    Maggie groans as she joins them at the bar. “Can you give her something better to do with that mouth, Lena?”

    “Yeah, Lena,” Kara teases, leaning in towards Lena’s lips. “Surely, you can come up with some genius plan.”

    “I can’t believe you’ve tricked the world into thinking you’re humble.”

    “If I remember correctly,” Kara licks her lips. “You actually couldn’t keep your hands off the cocky Kara Danvers.”

    Lena is saved by the appearance of more of the group.

    “What took you guys so long?” Alex asks. “I turned around and you were gone.”

    “We were just making out,” Kara covers. “Lena couldn’t keep her hands off of me—”

    “—That is absolutely not true.”

    Alex scowls. “You know, I think I preferred it when you two were hiding from everyone.”

    “And who thought all it would take to make badass Alex Danvers whine is her sister getting a little action?” Lena taunts.

    “Oh, okay. Just for that, Luthor, you’re coming up on stage with me first,” Alex threatens, waving a finger in Lena's face.

    “No, she’s not,” Kara intervenes, stepping a little closer to Lena — not that she's a flight risk or anything. “You’d really deny your sweet, little, baby sister the first song?”

    Alex snorts. “I wasn’t aware I had one of those.”

    Kara’s nose wrinkles up in faux offense.

    “Come on, come on,” Maggie says. She pulls away from the bar with her arms full of drinks and begins offloading some. “You two can duke it out at the table. Let's go.”

    “You always make Brainy sing with you, and it’s terrible, every time,” Alex complains at Kara. “I'd need to have a lot of alcohol in my blood for that.”
