    “Some of us happen to like Brainy’s, erm, artistic style,” Kara defends. “Sure, maybe it's not super conventional singing, but that’s the great thing about karaoke! You’re just supposed to do your best.”

    “It’s like if slam poetry and podcasts had a baby,” Alex continues. “But unlike both of those, even the speaker knows it's bad.”

    “What is with your crusade against slam poetry?” Kara asks. “Is it because of Vicki Donahue? It is, isn’t it?”

    “No …!” Alex scoffs.

    “Enough,” Maggie cuts them off. “Alex, whiskey. Kara, beer. Both of you, go sing. Start us off.”

    “Fine, fine,” Alex agrees.

    Kara winks at Lena. “Ready to be serenaded?”

    “Absolutely not,” Lena turns impossibly paler. “Do not. I’m begging you.”

    “Begging? That’s hot,” Kara grins, and runs away towards the mic before Lena can catch her.

    It doesn’t take the Danvers sisters long to agree on a song. As usual, Alex grabs the mic while the DJ sets everything up.

    “This one is for my sister, Kara,” Alex announces to the room. “It’s her favorite song. She’s the most selfless, generous, incredible person I know. There would be no ‘future Dr. Alex Danvers’ without her. So, without further ado …”

    Alex signals to the DJ and away they go.

    Multicolored lights dance all over the room, but Kara can still pick out Lena’s face in the crowd. They haven’t been here long, but between the collective body heat and the adrenaline, Kara’s already sweating profusely. It’s more excitement than nerves. She knows every single word to the song, as if she was born with them built into her brain. The words just flow one right after another.

    Effortless. 

    It’s fun to watch Lena’s face throughout the night. She looks thoroughly impressed when Kara's the one singing, and hilariously unimpressed when Mike and Winn go. Admittedly, duets are not their thing.

    Soon enough, it’s time for another round, and Kara and Lena make their way over to the bar. It’s quiet enough to hold a conversation again.

    Kara swipes away a piece of hair stuck to her sweaty forehead and looks at Lena. “So, what do you think?”

    “You can sing , Kara,” Lena praises.

    Kara can feel the blood rush to her cheeks. “I’m okay. You’re being very kind though. I just think singing is fun.”

    “No, you have a genuine talent,” Lena states. “I’ve heard you sing under your breath before — but that — that was incredible.”

    Kara gives a bashful laugh. “Flatterer. Trying to get into my pants?”

    “When am I not?” Lena winks. Kara doesn’t think she could ever tire of seeing that. “I have an exceptional track record so far.”

    “And I’m okay with that,” Kara smirks and raises her eyebrows at Lena. “I like when you—”

    “—what can I get you?” the bartender interrupts.

    “Scotch on the rocks, top shelf.” Lena hands over her card in her typical smooth way, as if she and Kara weren’t just moments away from a rather R-rated line of conversation. She glances down at Kara’s hand. “Please. And a …”

    “Blue Hawaiian,” Kara finishes.

    “Coming right up, but it’ll be a minute,” the bartender says. “We’re slammed tonight.”

    “That’s alright.”

    “No worries!”

    The bartender rushes away, leaving the two of them in their own little bubble again.

    “I bet your lips are bright blue, darling,” Lena teases.

    “Are they?” Kara asks. She steps just a bit closer. Their faces are close enough that it wouldn’t be any effort for them to kiss.

    “I can’t tell,” Lena says. She runs a thumb over Kara’s bottom lip. “You’re lucky these lights make it look like a rainbow had a baby with a strobe light.”

    “Well, just in case my lips are blue, maybe you should help me clean them off.”

    “Maybe I should.” Lena gives Kara that look — upwards through hooded eyes, framed by the perfect amount of eyeliner — that makes Kara want to pledge her loyalty to whatever deity has brought her to this exact moment.

    Lena’s lips always do feel so divine.

    After they pull apart, Lena sets a hand over Kara’s pec. “I have a question.”

    “Yes?” Kara asks, twisting her head so that Lena’s talking directly into her ear. The look on Lena’s face looks more serious than flirting, so she wants to hear it correctly.

    “What Alex said earlier, about how there would be no 'future Dr. Alex Danvers' without you …” Lena trails off. “And how generous you are. It sounded kind of like—”

    “—like I’m paying for Alex to go to medical school?” Kara turns her head back so her and Lena’s eyes lock.  “I am.”

    Lena nods slowly. “Alright. I … I-if you don’t mind me asking, where are you getting the money from? That’s like 300,000 dollars, Kara.”

    “Yeah, I know,” Kara lets out a pained chuckle.

    “I’ve seen your apartment,” Lena continues. “Where are you coming up with that money from? You aren’t … are you declaring—”

    “No.” Kara gives Lena a firm, reassuring look. They’re both aware the window to declare for the NWBL draft isn’t closed yet. “No. It’s nothing like that. It’s—”

    Kara pauses while the bartender hands them their drinks. “Thank you.”

    “—No, it’s money I’ve had for awhile,” Kara continues. She takes a sip from her fresh drink, knowing the alcohol won’t be enough to numb that familiar tinge of pain in her chest. “It’s from my parents.”

    “Oh.” All the tension in Lena’s body dissipates, only to be replaced by worry as she starts rubbing at Kara’s hipbone. It’s a welcome comfort.

    “It’s okay,” Kara assures. “This has been my plan for a long time. It’s the money from my parents’ estate. Their savings, life insurance … Aunt Astra’s too. And once I turned 18, Kal helped me sell my parents’ land in Krypton too.”

    “I’m sorry,” Lena says. “I didn’t realize.”

    “I didn’t want to tell anyone and make Alex uncomfortable, but she seems fine with people knowing,” Kara explains. “When the Danvers first took me in, Eliza and Jeremiah refused any money. The money from my parents’, or any sort of help from Kal.”

    “Why?” Lena asks. She looks thoroughly befuddled, and Kara can’t help but wonder how transactional everything in the Luthor family is.

    “They wanted me to feel like they wanted me for me . They didn’t want me to feel reduced to a number,” Kara takes another sip of her drink. The sweetness contrasts sharply with their current subject matter. “So the plan became to save it to pay for my college, but then … I got a full academic ride to NCU.” 

    “Academic?” Lena bites her lower lip. Kara can’t help but smirk a little.

    “Academic. It’s a true miracle,” Kara says. She knows Lena loves her dearly as she is, but it is a significant ego boost whenever Lena gets reminded of just how smart Kara actually is, and immediately looks ready to mount her.

    “So if you haven’t used it,” Lena states. “Then you still have all of that money.”

    Kara nods. “Since we don’t have enough time for part-time jobs, Eliza insisted on paying for my other college expenses too, along with Alex’s. I took a little for my savings — can’t buy sex toys on your adoptive mom’s dime, but—”

    Lena chokes on her drink.

    “—but,” Kara lets out a little laugh. “Otherwise it’s gone untouched. It took a lot of convincing to get Alex on board with using it for her medical school, but eventually I won.”

    “Congratulations,” Lena teases.

    “Thank you, it was very hard,” Kara’s voice gets raspy with pointed exasperation. She goes back to her normal voice and continues, “You know how stubborn Alex is. But to me, it’s a clear decision. If everything goes right, I won’t need that money in the league, and I can do something right with it this way.”

    “How so?”

    “I only have that money because my parents lost their lives,” Kara shrugs. “Alex is going to be a brilliant doctor one day. She’s going to save peoples’ lives. I thought it seemed only right that it be used to help her get to that point.”

    Lena nods sagely, looking at Kara with soft eyes.

    “Come on, this is supposed to be a fun night,” Kara nudges her shoulder at Lena. “Enough tragic backstory. Let’s dance!”

    Kara grabs Lena’s hand before she has a chance to protest and pulls them into the next room. It’s impossible to tell how big the room is, given how many people are shoved up against each other, but it's hot . The heat hits Kara’s skin like a wall.

    “It’s hot in here,” Kara announces to Lena. Does Lena definitely already know that? Yes. Does Kara need a convenient excuse to unbutton a few more buttons of her shirt? Also yes.

    Lena rolls her eyes. “This would be a terrible night for the fire marshal to swing by. They would love how much it is clearly up to code.”

    “And then shut the whole thing down?” Kara teases. “Trying to escape, Lena?”

    “Kara, I’m not really much of a dancer,” Lena protests. “I-I don’t know what to do.”

    “It’s okay, I’ve got you,” Kara's voice thrums low in her throat, and she’d be a liar if she said she didn’t notice the way Lena always reacts to that drop in octave. “Trust me?”

    “I-I do,” Lena agrees. 

    “It’s easy,” Kara promises. “I’ll teach you how to two-step. Turn around.”

    Lena does so, pressing her back against Kara’s chest. Kara’s hand settles on Lena’s hip and pulls their bodies close enough that there wouldn’t be enough air to breathe with left between them. Kara quickly transfers her drink from one hand to the other so that their cups don’t clink and spill. 

    Bodies press in all around them in the dim lighting. It’s total anonymity.

    “No one can see you.” Kara starts them off by just swaying along to the music. “Do you feel the rhythm of the song?”

    “I … I think so,” Lena says. She doesn’t sound very confident, but in Kara’s personal opinion, Lena Luthor looks hot enough that the quality of her dancing has no bearing on the situation. Plus, there’s something to be said for trial by fire.

    “At the beginning of the next line, take your right foot and step right. Kind of like a lunge, but shorter,” Kara directs. She mimics the motion, but smaller, so Lena can get the feel of it. “Then bring your left foot towards the right, but keep going past the back of your right foot, then plant it.”

    “And now that your legs are crossed, quickly step right to open your legs again,” Kara continues. “Bring your left foot up about halfway, then stomp it back down in the same spot it was.”

    Kara feels Lena’s leg jerk with the impact of the ground. “Good! Now step left and open your legs.”

    “Your desires are so subtle, darling,” Lena teases.

    “Ha-ha,” Kara snorts in her ear. “Same thing this side, but you’ll cross behind with your right, step left, and then stomp with your right.”

    “Easy,” Lena says sarcastically.

    “Just think of it like footwork,” Kara says. “You had to do footwork for fencing, right?”

    Lena makes a confirmatory groan. “Mm-mhm.”

    “It’s okay, remember, no one can see us,” Kara reassures. “Let's just try a few times.”

    They shift back and forth to the beat, Kara leading and Lena trying her best to follow along.

    “Drink more,” Kara encourages. “You’re too stiff. You’re thinking too hard. It’s just a feeling; it’s like having sex.”

    “Is that so?” comes Lena’s wry response.

    “Yes.”

    They shift back and forth a few more times. Lena starts to get more on rhythm with the next song that plays. At the end of one of the stepping sequences, Kara decides to add in another step.

    “Good! Now, Lena,” Kara whispers low into Lena’s ear. “When we get — here — roll your hips. Like I'm inside of you and you’re trying to kill me.”

    Kara’s hands guide Lena’s hips through the motion, but they don’t really serve any purpose other than selfish ones. Lena's already gotten the hang of it.

    “Is this really part of the dance?” Lena asks. “Or are you just an opportunist?”

    “Both,” Kara says. “Like I said, it’s like sex. It comes from the hips.”

    “You’re not so bad at this, Danvers,” Lena says. “But I’ve had enough of this for now.”

    “Okay, we can take a brea—” but before Kara can finish, she’s halted by the feeling of Lena Luthor straight-up grinding her incredible ass on Kara's body.

    Okay! Way better option!

    The heat between them seems to grow impossibly warmer. Almost in response, Lena hinges at the hip and presses her ass back against Kara even more. Kara grabs at Lena’s hipbone and holds her tight.

    Lena swings back up so their torsos are pressed together again. She tilts her head so her mouth is closer to Kara’s ear.

    “So Kara Danvers can sing and dance,” Lena remarks. “Is there anything she can’t do?”

    “Mmm … I could say the same thing about you, Lena, you’re so hot,” Kara murmurs. “I would give you anything you could ask for.”

    “Well, Danvers,” Lena sighs, tension evaporating off her shoulders. “Seeing as how we’ve been dancing for a while now, I suppose that makes two of us.”

    Kara finds words to be painfully insufficient to relay to Lena just how attractive this whole gambit is, so Kara chooses to nibble on Lena’s ear instead.

    “Don’t do that,” Lena warns. Her hand finds Kara’s thigh.

    “Don’t do what?”

    “Start something you can’t finish.”

    “Who said I can’t finish it?” Kara dares.

    “Oh really?” Lena asks. Her hand slides further up Kara’s thigh, shifting tantalizingly close to the apex of her legs, and squeezes the chunk of muscle. “Care to make good on that, Danvers?”

    Kara’s face breaks into a wide grin. “Let's get out of here, Luthor.”

    Life goes on.

    The peaceful silence is a utopia at first, but like all good things — it ends.

    A few days after karaoke, the news Lena’s been dreading seeing in headline form finally breaks. Guess they needed a little more time to ruin her life or something. She can’t be certain that Lex didn’t try and mettle a little, but honestly she doesn’t have the energy to care anymore.

    It becomes the lifeblood of every trashy gossip media outlet. 

    The first morning after the news breaks, her day begins relatively quiet. But then again, Lena is often up and studying in the Natural Sciences building before most alarm clocks go off. 

    But this isn't just any normal day. She’s unsure of what will greet her when she leaves the building to go to her next lecture. 

    It’ll be fine. She can do this. She’s already spent the morning pretending like she doesn’t notice the heads turn after her, the whispers behind her as she sits in class. It’s an old routine at this point.

    She concentrates hard on not walking out of the building too quickly — unwilling to let her anxiety show to the outside world.

    There’s a familiar face outside.

    On the list of people Lena would’ve expected to be waiting for her outside of the building, Mike Matthews slurping a cup of coffee was not on that list.

    “ ‘sup Lena,” Mike tilts his chin at her in a greeting. 

    “Hi, Mike,” Lena says, both of them pretending like people aren't openly staring at them.

    “Can I walk with you?” Mike asks, taking another slurp of coffee.

    “... Sure,” Lena agrees, not quite certain where this is heading. “ … I’m heading to Tower Hall.”

    “Oh, oh, I know where that one is!” Mike looks a little too proud of himself for knowing where a basic, heavily-utilized lecture hall is. It makes Lena question his attendance record. “I went to a mental health seminar there that was actually really cool.”

    They begin to walk off together.

    “So,” Lena inhales. “Can I ask why you’re on this side of campus? I was under the impression you weren’t the biggest fan of going to class.”

    "Oh, I'm not going to class. I didn't come here to play classes," Mike jokes, then grows more sober. “I heard about your, uh, family stuff.”

    “That quickly?” Lena feigns surprise. She hasn’t looked for herself, but she would imagine the news of her true parentage is pervasive on most gossip pages now.

    “I spend too much time on my phone,” Mike says. “ … So how are you doing?”

    “I’m fine,” Lena sighs. “People talking about my family is nothing new.”

    “It’s still unfair to you,” Mike says. “I hate it every time my mom runs in a new election … they always dig out a ton of shit about me. All the dumb things I’ve ever done, just trying to live my life — it’s a pretty long list.”

    “... Yes, it’s not my favorite,” Lena admits to him.

    “I know how much it sucks to have people watching you, talking shit about you when you walk by,” Mike offers. “I wasn’t sure what the crowd would look like today but I just thought it would be nice to not be alone.”

    Lena almost stops in her tracks. That explains Mike’s presence quite logically, but the sentiment is … unexpected. But certainly not unwelcome.

    “Oh, I’m not alone,” Lena remarks. “The hulking man wearing all black, about a hundred feet behind us? That’s Finch, my brother’s personal security guard.”

    “Oh, woah,” Mike whips his head around in search of Finch. “That’s a little creepy. Is your brother here?”

    “No, he’s back in Metropolis by now,” Lena says. “I’ve inferred that he left Finch behind to watch out for me.”

    “I, uh, guess it’s good he cares that you’re safe?”

    “We’re not exactly on speaking terms right now,” Lena says. “But I suppose so.”

    “No wonder it’s been pretty chill so far,” Mike says. “My mom’s security is tough but that dude looks scary as shit.”

    “He’s less frightening after you’ve seen him sneeze so hard his head hits the table in front of him,” Lena says.

    Mike’s jaw drops open. “No … no way! That dude? Did the table break?”

    Lena shakes her head. “But yes, it’s been surprisingly tame so far. I’m surprised there hasn’t been someone jumping out of the bushes yet,” Lena says.

    Mike chuckles. “Oh, there were. Public Safety came by while I was waiting and cleared them out. Gotta make sure that your future hefty alumni donation is still on the table. Guess they got lucky it was just the donut patrol and not your brother’s bodyguard.”

    Lena tries to hide her surprise at the fact that Mike had not only thought to walk her to class, but had actually shown up early and waited for her.  “Were you waiting for a while?”

    “Nah, not long,” Mike says. “If I ever end up working a job that gets me handcuffed to a golf cart by a college public safety officer, I think I’d quit on the spot.”

    Well, that’s quite the insight into today’s campus happenings.

    “Lofty career goals,” Lena teases. "You seem to have a particular distain for Public Safety."

    Mike groans. “Oh, yeah. Dickheads. They've given me a lot of parking tickets."

    Rather than touch on Mike's mutual involvement in such a scenario, Lena just laughs politely.

    “Thank you for this,” she says, as they approach the entrance to Tower Hall. “It was a lovely surprise.”

    “For sure,” Mike shrugs. “I’ve been there. And for what it’s worth, no one will care tomorrow.”

    Lena gives a skeptical huff.

    “Well, maybe in a few days,” Mike blinks a few times. “Apparently, you’re very popular.”

    “I don't believe anyone has ever called me that.”

    “Hey, it’s never too late for a miracle!”

    Lena laughs for real this time and shakes her head at him, taking a few steps towards the front door.

    Mike gives her a lazy two-fingered salute. “Later, boss.”

    True to Mike’s prediction, it passes. 

    The world stops caring soon after the Luthors do, and Lena loses her hulking shadow, recalled back to Lex’s side. There’s always a more exciting story out there to move on to.

    The hardest pill to swallow in the whole thing ends up being when Lena’s therapist tells her: ‘You can’t speed your way through emotional processing, Lena. Healing and acceptance takes time.’

    So patience it is.

    Indeed, everything begins to feel decidedly regular again with time. Kara and Lena figure out how to balance their new relationship, making time for each other and also for themselves.

    Lena never misses another class that semester. She still spends what Kara considers an ‘ungodly’ amount of time working on assignments and studying for exams, but she doesn’t mind. Science is just as much her home as her apartment is.

    Rather than be a distracting menace while Lena tries to work, Kara throws herself into her physical therapy, giving it the dedication of an athlete who, as Lena would describe it: ‘can’t do their favorite thing in the world, but fuck if they don’t have an annoying amount of energy to burn on something, anything.’

    Lena also finds joy in fencing again. It’s just as much an outlet for frustration as it is for fun, but she’s okay with that. Jack and Andrea provide great emotional support, excuses to unearth from her textbooks, and lovely wine nights. 

    She and Mike begin an unlikely friendship borne of mutual understanding (and a smidge of weed). On the weekends, Maggie teaches her little bits of Spanish when they go out drinking, and it becomes a game to see how much Lena remembers over breakfast the next day. Alex starts teasing her like only an older sibling can.

    Everything is almost perfect, save one looming elephant in the room: the NWBL Draft declaration deadline.

    They don’t talk about it. Lena knows Kara is staying, she does, but it’s unclear if the deadline will pass over them with a bang or with a whimper. But her trepidation only lingers for so long before it’s dropped in the name of energy conservation, and Lena doesn’t even realize today is the day until she's scrolling through social media on an early morning coffee break.

    It’s a post from Kara.

    But it’s not a photo of Kara — it's a photo of a photo, crinkled and aged, of two young adults. The woman on the left has dark brown hair, glasses held aloft on shapely cheekbones, and a polished smile. The smile of the man beside her is crooked but warmer. He has blonde hair and a stubborn jaw, and the same pair of steel blue eyes that Lena knows all so well.

    Kara’s parents.

    The caption underneath reads: ‘Hello everyone. Today is the last day for players to declare for the NWBL Draft. But half of you following me probably already knew that … Ever since I was little, I’ve wanted to be one of those players, and today I want it even more than ever. But I’m staying to finish my fourth year at NCU, and it’s because of these people right here. I got some good advice to start talking about them more. So if you want to know my story, who the real Kara Danvers is, please read it here—

    Lena clicks on the link so quickly it could border on superspeed.

    The title of the article is overshadowed in favor of a bright image of Kara: in her basketball uniform, black fabric draped over her shoulders, holding up a silver trophy in her right hand. It’s a magnet for light.

    NCU Comets point guard Kara Danvers (11) holds up the National Championship’s Most Outstanding Player Award at Garden Stadium in Gateway City, CA. Danvers’ championship performance once again helped the Comets clinch their second National Title in three years.

    Beneath that, a brick of text:

    . . . . . . . 

    By: James Olsen

    National City, CA — National City University basketball player Kara Danvers, well-known by the nickname ‘Supergirl’, has been the delight of college basketball fans for the past three years. She has an impressive list of accomplishments:  Rookie of the Year, numerous conference accolades, team MVP, and this year’s national tournament’s Most Outstanding Player — the same tournament in which Danvers clinched her second national championship. Given her decorated history, it’s no wonder Danvers’ status in the NWBL Draft has been an area of constant speculation.

    Like most players with the potential to go into the professional leagues, Danvers had wanted to do a One-and-Done at first. (‘One-and-Done’ is a term commonly used to describe college players that play college basketball for one year to become eligible for either NBL draft.) But now three years into her career at NCU, that obviously didn’t happen.

    The sport has flourished in the era following pay-equality. NWBL rookie contracts mean drafted players can earn several million dollars a year, a rather difficult opportunity for most people to decline. Danvers has opted instead to wait — three times over. 

    So now, on the last day of eligibility to declare for this year’s draft, Danvers sat down with me to set the record straight:

     

    Playing professional basketball is an incredible opportunity. Why wait?

    “I play basketball because I love it, first and foremost,” Danvers said. “That kind of money can touch people’s lives in so many ways and I don’t want to ignore or dismiss that fact. Everyone’s reasons for playing are valid. But for me, it’s a bit more complicated, and that’s why I’ve held off from declaring for the draft just yet.”

    Speculation regarding the Girl of Steel’s draft status is nothing new; it’s occurred like clockwork every college basketball season that Kara Danvers has played. This year has been no different, but with her sister and teammate — Alex Danvers — graduating this spring,  it would seem like there’s not much left to keep Supergirl here at National City.

    “I know there’s been a lot more speculation this year,” Danvers said. “I haven’t always been the most clear about my plans. There’s been a lot of factors weighing in, and it’s been a bit complicated at times.”

     

    Why not declare for the NWBL Draft?

    “Honestly? … Because of my, uh, my parents,” Danvers admitted.  This version of Kara Danvers is different than what most know. She spoke softly, shoulders rolled inwards, with a vulnerability in her eyes. 

    “They passed away when I was thirteen,” Danvers said. It’s a relatively unknown fact, which Danvers has kept to a quite close circle, until now. 

    Eight years ago, Danvers’ childhood home in Krypton, Alaska, caught fire one December night. Her mother, father, and aunt all perished. Danvers was spared after being knocked unconscious at the entryway of the house. Barely anything was left behind in the ruins.

    “I don’t talk about my parents a lot,” she stated. “It’s really hard for me. But I got some good advice that I should start talking about them more, and I want to do that. I want pieces of them to still be out in the world.”

     

    What do you want the world to know about them?

    “That they were here and they're a part of me,” Danvers said. “They were complex … but good parents. My mom would always help with my homework, no matter how tired she was. And my dad — he was my first ever basketball coach.”

    Danvers started playing basketball at age seven.

    “I was a pretty energetic kid,” Danvers chuckled. “I had a lot of energy to burn, and he was hoping basketball would be a good way to do it. I’d like to think it worked, but … I’m probably biased, who knows?”

    Danvers’ recovery is smooth, but the original words still hang in the room; a constant for anyone who’s ever lost a parent: '… and I can’t ask him to know for sure.'

    “Losing my family was the hardest thing I’ve ever gone through,” Danvers said. “But there’s so many people out there who go through similar adversity and so I hope talking about it more will help others.”

     

    So how do your parents factor into your draft decision now?

    Danvers chuckled with a dose of self-deprecation. “I can be a bit stubborn. And maybe a bit reckless. When I was a kid, I was insistent on becoming a professional basketball player. I didn’t want to hear anything else.”

    Danvers goes on to inform us that while she came from a very loving family, there had been a lack of support for her career dreams.

    “I think they were concerned, like any parent would be,” Danvers said. “When it comes to people you love, you want them to have an easy and happy life. I know they were worried that  I would be disappointed or hurt. That my life would just be filled with adversity and heartbreak.”

     

    You’re clearly a very talented basketball player. Did that not help support your case?

    Danvers laughed the compliment off. “I wasn’t always. I was a bit awkward in my body; not quite sure how to use it. I think natural talent does matter some, but I also put in a lot of hard work and practice. It wasn’t until a few years after my parents passed away that I got really good at basketball.”

    “I used to practice shooting for hours,” Danvers said. “It would help me clear my head. I think it’s meditative in a way … it’s really all you can focus on. The rest would sort of fade away — that I was having a hard time making friends at my new school, that I felt full of more emotions that I could possibly identify, and that I missed my parents and my home so much .” 

    After the tragic loss of her family, Danvers was adopted by Eliza and Jeremiah Danvers, the biological parents of NCU’s own Alex Danvers. (Kara would later take the family surname.)

    “Moving to Midvale [CA] and living with the Danvers was a bit of a culture-shock,” Danvers said. “I grew up in a pretty desolate region of Alaska. Seeing Midvale for the first time — it was so green and lush. It blew my mind. I was grieving and growing up and just really overwhelmed with a lot of everyday life. It felt like I crash-landed on a whole new planet, in a way.”

     

    How did you adjust to this new ‘world’?

    “I missed my biological parents a lot, and I still do,” Danvers said. “I was so lucky to find my second family in the Danvers — my sister, Alex, and parents, Eliza and Jeremiah. But it wasn’t always easy at first. It took time and effort to get there.”

    Their mother Eliza runs a research lab hours away in Midvale, CA, often live-streaming her daughters’ games in the lab conference room. Their father Jeremiah passed away a few years ago following a heart attack. He worked as Clark Kent’s first basketball agent before taking an early retirement to raise his daughters. 

    “Jeremiah was always very supportive of me playing basketball,” Danvers said. “He had built a little basketball court in our backyard, and would spend hours out there with Alex and I, going as long as we wanted to go for — typically until Eliza called us in for dinner, she’s an amazing cook — but anyway, he was—”

    Danvers paused to take a breath.

    “—he was a great man,” Danvers stated, her tone heavy with emotion. “Alex is a lot like him. Losing him really cemented our bond as sisters. Having someone to grieve together with really helps. It’s a lonely process, but in my experience, it's feeling that support and strength from someone else that helps you heal. So you can be stronger for them and for yourself. And kudos to Eliza — she was really our rock through the whole thing. She’s worked so hard to give us both a good life.”

     

    So how do all of your family figures factor into your decision to finish at NCU before moving to the league?

    “I’ve always wanted to go pro, as young as I can remember. But everyone has encouraged me to wait until I get my degree,” Danvers said. “My parents had very strong feelings about it. The Danvers’ have shown more unconditional support of it, but there was certainly a bit of caution and advice-giving any time I considered declaring early.”

     

    Did anyone else’s advice factor into your decision-making process?

    Danvers paused to give the room a knowing look. “If you’re asking about [Clark Kent] — he was your typical big-brother about it.”

    Clark Kent is Danvers’ biological cousin, better known to the world as the basketball superstar ‘Superman’. Famous for his skills on the court, he’s also known to be a humble and generous philanthropist, social rights advocate, and part-time farmer in the off-season. But to Kara Danvers, he’s basically an older brother — and the only biological family either of them have left.

    After the loss of Kara’s parents, the two kept in touch to the best of their abilities: Kara would watch all of his games, and they would message frequently. Clark would fly Kara out to visit Metropolis during her summer break and his off-season. But to him, school always came first.

    “[Clark] wanted me to stay and finish my degree,” Danvers said. “It’s what he did. I think he’s more patient than I am, but he always says he was just as reckless when he was my age. But I think I’ve got him beat; he was pretty exasperated trying to convince me not to One-and-Done after my first year.”

     

    So to recap, your biological parents, your adopted parents, and your cousin all advised you to stay and finish your degree before going to the professional leagues. But you weren’t convinced?

    “Yeah, basically,” Danvers chuckled. “Like I said, I’m pretty stubborn. I was your typical nineteen-year-old with that burning need to make my own decisions. But it runs deeper than that. I feel like I belong as a basketball player. I feel at home on that court. I want to be out there for as long as I possibly can.”

    “I almost did it too,” Danvers said. “I got about as close to declaring for the draft as you can.”

     

    So then why didn’t you end up doing a One-and-Done, if even Superman couldn’t convince you?

    “Alex. My sister,” Danvers answered. “She’s the one that got me to buy-in, but indirectly.”

    Even though they don’t share blood, Kara and Alex Danvers share an unquantifiable amount of sisterly love.

    “After we won our first national championship my freshman year, I started to see things differently,” Danvers said. “Basketball feels like home to me, but so does Alex. Having both at the same time was something too good to pass up. I was more open to staying; I told myself I could wait another season before declaring.”

    “But then of course, we lost in the semi-finals last year,” Danvers said. “I was pissed. You can say what you want to about that game — the play, the refs, the injuries — but regardless, I felt that it was unfinished business. So I stayed for another year. I wanted to win another championship with Alex.”

     

    What was it like to win not one, but two championships alongside your sister?

    Danvers immediately smiled bright enough to outshine every light in the room. 

    “There’s no feeling like it,” Danvers described, eyes full of nostalgic joy. “The feeling of working so hard for something, wanting it more than words can describe, then achieving it? That’s an incredible feeling. But to do it together with someone I love, to share that feeling — it’s indescribable.”

     

    So your sister got you to buy in, but she’s now graduating. What are you staying for?

    “My degree.” Danvers lets out a notably long exhale. 

    “Because I’ve grown up,” Danvers continued. “I was resistant to doing what my parents wanted of me for a long time. Alex bought me time, and in that time I’ve matured and realized more about them and the world.”

    “I’ve started to understand why my parents wanted it for me so badly,” Danvers said. “They saw my degree as an assurance of a good future. While I disagree somewhat with that premise, I’m not a fool. I’m so lucky to even have the means to go to school. Going pro is something I want — so badly — but I’ve realized this is something I need to do first. 

     

    Why?

    “I want my parents, the Danvers, Clark, Alex, everyone who loves me to be proud of me,” Danvers said. “There’s a major self-imposed pressure that comes with that … but I’m learning the best way to make someone who truly loves you proud is to be the real you. So I’m trying to be the real Kara Danvers. More open to the world.”

    At the beginning of the interview, Danvers' body language was tense and protective. True to her words, she now sits with a calmness and an openness, which echo the truth to her words.

    “Finishing my degree is for closure. It’s to honor my parents and the love I have for them, in a way,” Danvers finished. “I’ve learned you can feel two things at once. My feelings about my family are complicated and they can stay that way. This is something I’ve realized that I just need to do for myself.”

     

    Now, what comes next for Kara Danvers?

    “Next season, of course,” Danvers grinned. She leaned forward in a conspiratorial manner. “I think three is a great number, don’t you?”

    Danvers followed her comment with a confident wink, before setting back into her earnest manner.

    “I’ll miss Alex and our other seniors that are moving on. Everyone will. But I’m so excited for her to start medical school and begin the next phase of her life. She’s worked so hard for it and I’m so proud of her,” Danvers said. “And I’m lucky to have such a great group of teammates to play with next year. The Comets will be just as stellar as always.”

     

    Was that a pun?

    “A pretty good one, if you ask me,” Danvers said, soaking in self-satisfied delight.

     

    Kara Danvers will officially return to National City University to use her final year of eligibility to play college ball and graduate with a degree in journalism.

    “I can’t wait to enter the league,” Danvers promised. “This is just something I have to do first.”

    The Comets season will begin next October.

    People have been looking at Kara differently all day. Maybe it’s just in her head. Or maybe lots of them read her article. It’s hard to tell if people are looking her way because it’s human instinct to track movement, or because she bared more of her soul than she’s ever dared to before. And posted about it. She’s not used to attention invoked by vulnerability instead of heroics.

    It makes her skin itch.

    Kara’s impressed by how quickly Lena finds the article. Usually she doesn’t have time for social media until her afternoon coffee break. Must be a slow day in the world of Lena I-have-eight-different-majors Luthor.
