    Direct Message from psionchic: Hey, this is gayle marsh, I play for midway unv. I lost my mom a few months ago. I saw your article and just wanted to say it was nice to hear someone like me talk about how hard losing a parent is. It's nice to know i'm not alone.

    And that’s not the only one. Kara’s inbox is full by the end of the day with messages of support, from people all over sharing their own experiences with loss and grief and resilience.

    For the first time since her parents’ death, Kara feels how big the world is — but in the best way.

    The rest of the school year comes and goes. 

    It’s the typical flurry that occurs every spring: classes, projects, exams, papers, notebooks, long nights in the library, exams again … and on and on it goes. But Lena doesn’t really mind. She’s always been inclined to avoid people, but certainly more so after this cataclysm of a year.

    However, where the world has pushed her out to sea, Kara and company have pulled her back to safety. Kara’s friends have fully welcomed her into the fold. On this particular night, a few of them — Lena, Kara, Mike, and Winn — are sitting around on the rooftop of Kara’s apartment complex, killing time by sharing a joint.

    Mike holds the unlit joint aloft, as if it was a campaign glass.

    “To Kara!” he cheers. “For your article with James. It’s badass to talk about your feelings.”

    Even in the darkness, Lena can see Kara’s face flush red from the unwanted attention.

    “To Kara.”

    Mike lights the joint with practiced ease and takes the first toke, as is his right. He then holds it out to Kara.

    “Nah, I’m okay,” Kara then passes it along to Lena. “But thank you. Lena?”

    “Sure.” Lena brings the joint to her lips and gives a good inhale. The back of her throat feels like dry coals as she holds her breath, then exhales. Smoke goes into the air. 

    “I saw in the news that your mom’s officially running for re-election,” Kara informs Mike, as Lena passes the joint along to Winn.

    “ Oh yeah ,” Mike sighs. “Here we go again.”

    “Maybe this time won’t be as bad?” Winn says. “Just one more year and then you can graduate and move away.”

    “Ooh, yeah,” Kara nods along. “Maybe a nice remote cabin in the woods?

    Mike makes a disgusted face. “There’s no bars or clubs there. What would I do for fun? How would I get laid? How would I get weed?”

    “You could grow your own, city boy,” Kara teases Mike. 

    His expression changes to something pensive. “That’s not a bad idea,” he agrees.

    “How long has your mother been a senator for?” Lena asks.

    “Since I was fifteen,” Mike replies. “Thank fuck this is her last election. Hopefully.”

    Lena nods in sympathy. 

    “I’m sorry Mike. Have you talked to your dad?” Kara asks. “What does he think about it?”

    “I don’t know, the usual,” Mike mumbles. “We both know Queen Rhea always gets her way. Doesn’t matter how many people she makes miserable on the way.”

    “Our mothers could co-teach a class on that,” Lena says.

    “Fun Sponges 101?” Kara suggests. 

    Lena chuckles. “I was thinking more in the vein of ‘how to be a raging bitch'—no offense, Mike—”

    “—none taken, she is one—”

    “—but ‘fun sponge’ is perhaps a more polite term,” Lena finishes.

    “I like it, ” Winn agrees.

    “You know who would be the first person to sign up for that class?” Mike points the joint out at no one in particular. “Veronica Sinclair. Not that she needs any practice.”

    “Ooh, and Siobhan!” Winn adds. “She’s so mean.”

    Kara’s face is all scrunched up in pain and regret. “Can we please stop naming my exes,” she begs. “Please. I get it, I had poor decision making skills my first two years here.”

    “Sorry.”

    The conversation pauses as Winn has a little coughing fit. 

    “I’m good, I’m good,” he assures the group.

    Lena takes her next hit and exhales, watching the smoke meet the air.

    She's always enjoyed the sight of smoke. Maybe it’s the familiarity, from Lionel’s cigars or Lex’s blunts. Or maybe it’s how the wisps defy the gravity of their surroundings, flowing upwards into nothing, always an ethereal dance.

    Fortune favors the brave.

    That’s what they say right?

    Maybe it’s just the weed, but on this particular night, Lena has decided to do the unthinkable: ask these new friends for their help.

    “Can I get your opinions on something?” Lena blurts out. Kara gives her a curious look.

    Mike and Winn both nod, also looking a bit puzzled.

    “My mother wants to see me,” Lena says. “She’s been trying for a while; with the lawyers, with Lex …”

    Everyone freezes for a second, until Mike coughs and breaks the silence. “Wait, like in prison?”

    “Yes.”

    “What do you think she wants?” Kara asks, passing the joint along from Winn to Lena.

    “I don’t know." Lena takes a hit and exhales.

    A cold breeze passes over them as Lena hands the joint to Winn. “And I don’t care. I just thought I was done with all of this. With her.”

    Winn nods in support.

    “But I can’t say I wouldn’t have a few choice words to tell her,” Lena admits.

    “Uh,” Kara stammers. “I …”

    Winn looks equally as lost. Mike counts to three on his fingers.

    “I shouldn’t feel guilty for not wanting to see her, right?” Lena asks.

    Mike shakes his head. “No. What would make you feel guilty?”

    “I don’t know,” Lena lets out a long exhale. “It’s just that she’s my mother … more or less. Family is supposed to count for something, isn’t it?”

    “In my experience, family is chosen,” Kara says. “Family are all the people that choose to treat you with love. It’s not limited to blood.”

    “Lillian and I don’t share blood anyway,” Lena remarks.

    “That’s not a bad thing,” Winn murmurs. “I wish I was less related to my dad.”

    “You’re not your dad, Winn,” Kara assures. “You’re your own person and you make your own choices.”

    "Like not killing people?" Winn retorts.

    “Yeah, besides, you could argue it’s the whole nature-versus-nurture thing, right?” Mike asks. “Your mom’s great, Winn. She helped you turn out right.”

    Winn chuckles awkwardly and squirms a bit on his makeshift crate seat, as if he’s not used to receiving verbal affection from Mike. “That’s the hope.”

    Mike lets out a long exhale of smoke, trying and failing to blow it in a pattern. He waves the smoke away and passes the joint along.

    “Well, Lena, if you end up wanting to visit her, I’ve done the prison visitation paperwork before,” Winn volunteers. “It’s a little annoying to fill out, but I’m happy to help you, if you want.”

    “I … Thank you, Winn,” Lena bows her head. “I’m not really one to reinvent the wheel.”

    Winn gives her a soft smile.

    Lena’s far too aware that Kara’s been watching her this entire time, with soft but exacting eyes. However soft, it’s not quite enough to hide the presence of an opinion.

    “And what do you think?” Lena asks Kara.

    “I …Well, do you think going would be helpful for you? For your peace of mind?” Kara asks.

    Mike hums. “You could tell her how you really feel.”

    “She’s been the same way my entire life,” Lena says. “I’m not sure what possible difference there would be now that would cause her to suddenly give a shit about what I have to say.”

    “I read …” Mike’s cough breaks this sentence. “Read something somewhere recently that ‘it’s hard to speak up for yourself when it feels like no one is listening’. But you still hear your own voice, even if no one does.”

    “I think Mike’s right,” Kara says. The lines of her mouth twist around with excess emotion. Her eyes are far away from the moment, back in another time. “I’ve spent a lot of my life wishing I could speak to my parents again. What I want to say to them changes all the time. But regardless of what it’s about — I can’t tell them.”

    “Lillian is still here,” Kara continues. “You can still talk to her, if that would bring you peace. Tell her how you feel. For you.”

    “Yeah …” Lena sighs. “Maybe so. I’ll think about it. Thank you, all three of you.”

    Maybe I’ll just procrastinate making my decision until I die, Lena thinks. That’s a perfectly valid strategy.

    But before she can ruminate in the thicket any longer, she’s saved by Maggie throwing the rooftop stairway door open and yelling at them to get their asses inside now. “You guys are still up here!? The show is starting, and Khaleesi waits for no one!”

    Apparently, Maggie Sawyer doesn’t either.

    It takes a few weeks — on the dot, actually — for Lena to announce her decision.

    It’s a Sunday night. Kara and Alex hold their typical watch party for Game of Thrones, complete with drinks, snacks, and lots of praise for the beautiful dragon woman. 

    All the usual suspects attend. Alex, Maggie, Brainy, and Nia squeeze into their usual spots on the big couch. James and Lucy are squeezed into the other smaller one, tangled up so tightly that they’re practically engaged in coitus. Mike and Winn cap off the group, lounging on the floor in front of the TV.

    Kara plops down into her chair, perfectly molded to her favorite sitting position, and pulls Lena down into her lap.

    The familiar thrum of the episode opener vibrates through Kara’s chest.

    Lena’s silent throughout the entire episode, which isn’t uncommon, but there’s something slightly different about it this time. In an innate response, Kara rubs little soothing circles into Lena’s thigh.

    Kara won’t ask about it until everyone else has left. Thankfully, they filter out in small groups rather quickly, as if they can tell Kara wants them gone. Alex and Maggie are the last to leave. It’s then just the two of them, Kara and Lena, casually cleaning up discarded beer cans and trash left behind. 

    A sleepy silence has fallen over the room, and Kara wonders if she should just ask Lena another time. But something is clearly on Lena’s mind, so Kara should just probably just ask her. That seems like the healthy relationship thing to do. Right?

    Before Kara can figure out the answer, Lena speaks.

    “I’ve made up my mind,” Lena announces.

    Kara looks down at the empty container of buffalo chicken dip in her hand. “Uh, I’m sorry Lena, but I think the dip’s been gone for a while. We can get more for next Sunday and you can try it then?”

    Lena gives an amused snort and shakes her head. “Sorry, not that. I meant about visiting my Mom in Metropolis.”

    “Oh, phew,” Kara sighs. “Oh. Oh … what did you decide?”

    “I’m going,” Lena states. “Not for her. For me.”

    Kara gives her a gentle smile. Hopefully it’s a reassuring one. “I’m glad you figured out what’s best for you. I think it's brave.”

    “Thank you,” Lena grimaces. “I can’t believe I’m going to voluntarily get on a plane again. This is far exceeding my preferred annual flight total.”

    Kara chuckles. “I’ll go with you, if you want me to.”

    “I don’t want you to feel obligated,” Lena says.

    “I don’t.”

    “What about Alex’s graduation?” Lena asks.

    “There’s a week between the end of finals and graduation,” Kara says. “Alex and the other seniors on the team are planning on going to the beach to celebrate, so it’ll be pretty dead here anyway.”

    “I don’t want to keep you from Alex and your friends,” Lena states. “Wouldn’t you rather be there?”

    “Paying ridiculous cover charges to get into shitty bars, watching Alex and Maggie make out nonstop, and holding people’s hair while they puke into a bush on the side of the road?” Kara rattles off. “Not really. I’d rather go with you.”

    Lena seems to genuinely contemplate Kara’s offer, which is a relief; she thought she would have to try much harder to get Lena to agree.

    “We can go for the week and then be back for graduation, ” Kara suggests. “Since you were planning on staying in National City for the summer anyway, it works out.”

    "Oh, absolutely not. I plan on spending as little time there as I can, for the rest of forever," Lena says. "I … if you want to come, I would love to have you."

    “Then I’ll be there,” Kara promises. “I’ll always be there when you need me.”

    “I’ll pay for your ticket and everything,” Lena says. “I’ll send you my itinerary once I get it from Jess. But there will be a few things I’ll need to do on my own when we’re there.” 

    “Oh no,” Kara’s voice drips with sarcasm as she clutches at her heart. “I’ll have to keep myself entertained … in a city where Kal and Lois and Jon live … three of my favorite people in this world. Agony .” 

    Lena rolls her eyes and shakes her head.

    “It’ll be fine.” Kara brings her voice back to normal. “You can take all the time and space you need.”

    “Thank you … though maybe we could spend a little time together, all of us,” Lena suggests. “It would be nice to get to know your family more.”

    “I’d really like that,” Kara promises, her chest full of pleasant butterflies. She then gives Lena a wicked grin. “Plus, the Kents have a pool. You can all bear witness to the beginning of my hot girl summer.”

    Lena groans. (But it’s really more of a wistful moan, if you ask Kara.)

    “Hot. Girl. Sum-mer,” Kara enunciates, just in case Lena was too busy groaning the first time to hear it. “It’s happening, Lena. Get excited.”

     

    back to the beginning

    Chapter Summary

    The year reaches its end.

    Chapter Notes

    Thank you to every one who supported this story along the way — I can't thank you enough. Writing this and sharing it with you all was a real joy during a hard time for me, and many others too I'm sure. I think I've done enough writing for a bit; now it's time for me to do some reading. There's so many good stories and creators out there. But who knows, maybe a new story will come one day.

    The support you showed me truly means so much. I hope you all create your own happy endings. In the meantime, I present to you: Kara and Lena's ...

    It’s an irresistible, immeasurable force that’s pulled her here. Lena can’t quite explain it, but … well, here she is, now three thousand miles from home at a private prison in Metropolis.

    Ugh.

    “Well, look who decided to show up.”

    The concrete room is almost devoid of color, but Lena still sees red.

    “I can leave whenever I wish,” Lena states. “A freedom we don’t share. You clearly wanted me here for a reason, so I suggest you get to it.”

    “No, I—” Lillian sighs. She has the decency to look mildly regretful. “I’m sorry. I’m just under a bit of stress.”

    “I can’t imagine why.”

    “Yes, well,” Lillian lifts her eyebrows in a knowing gesture. “I promised myself to try and be better. Please, sit.”

    Lena hesitates for a moment. It’s only proper; one should always watch for traps before engaging with a Luthor. It’s often the only way to come out with minimal damage. But there’s no immediate discernible danger and Lena’s curiosity begs to be satisfied. She sits.

    “How are you doing, Lena?” comes the sickening-sweet voice of concern.

    Are you fucking kidding me? Lena thinks.

    “Don’t,” Lena bites. “You wanted me here for a reason. Why?”

    “... Fine. Let it be noted that I tried. I asked you here because I imagine you have questions,” Lillian says. “And I’m willing to answer them.”

    How benevolent.

    “Funnily enough, none are coming to mind.”

    “None come to mind,” Lillian corrects. “Your grammar has gotten sloppy. This is why it’s important to watch the company you keep.”

    “Yes, you’ve always been so concerned with the company I keep,” Lena snaps. “You truly can’t stand that I love women, don’t you?”

    Lillian gives Lena a sharp look. “I’ve grown. I think I have been more than tolerant of you and your little—”

    “—whatever word you’re about to use, I guarantee it won’t win you any favors,” Lena says. “Nothing was ever good enough for you, especially my romantic partners.”

    “I only tried to push you to be better,” Lillian says. “Is that not a parent’s job?”

    Lena scoffs. “How many of my relationships did you sabotage in the name of ‘making me better’?”

    “I admit, I made a mistake by interfering with your relationship with that one girl, but I’ve improved,” Lillian says.

    “Taylor. She has a name. People exist outside of what they can do for you,” Lena says. “And you didn’t interfere with my relationship, you broke it. I would hardly consider your tendency to flaunt me around to benefit Luthor Corp’s PR — only to later push whatever convenient man back on me — to be an ‘improvement’.”

    “You’re so sensitive,” Lillian sneers. “How the world hasn’t crushed that out of you, I don’t understand. Luthors cannot afford to be sensitive, Lena, it’s a weakness.”

    Lena’s first and only thought is of Kara. Who’s every bit the antithesis of Lillian’s statement.

    “Caring about other people isn’t a weakness,” Lena states. “You’ve just convinced yourself it is so that you don’t have to try.”

    Lillian’s eyes narrow and lips tighten, and she looks ready to laugh or scream. Lena’s not actually certain which.

    “Fine. You want the truth?” Lillian asks. “I don’t understand your choices, or you. Your father and I worked so hard for you and Lex to have a good life. You had everything you needed and you chose to make your life harder.”

    “It was never a choice!” Lena hisses. “I’ve had no choice in any of this! You never allowed me to be myself, from the moment I stepped foot in the Manor. I was only ever a piece in your game. Never good enough to be a Luthor, but I had to try, didn’t I? Because that’s all I could be to you.”

    “You’re ungrateful,” Lillian spits. “Do you have any idea what we’ve given to you?”

    “Do you have any idea what you’ve taken from me?” Lena retorts. “My entire life, you made me feel like an outsider. Like I didn’t belong. I would try so hard to be good enough for you, and still, I never was.”

    “I was trying to make you act like a Luthor,” Lillian says. “I tried to protect you, believe it or not.” 

    “Protect me?” Lena repeats, as if it's the most ridiculous sentiment she’s ever heard. “Is that why you hid that paternity test from me? In the name of protection?”

    The air in the room freezes.

    Lillian glares at Lena, eyes blazing across the metal table, and yet, Lena doesn’t feel a thing. It’s not directed at her. Instead, it’s as if Lillian is staring right through her — eyes spewing hatred at nothing but a ghost.

    “Do you know how I found out about your father’s affair?” 

    It’s rhetorical. 

    “Our marriage had begun to crumble a few years after Lex was born. He pulled away from me. He treated me as if I was there solely to make his life more difficult. But I didn’t want to give up on our life together. So I surprised him on one of his business trips.”

    Lena’s stomach twists in a slight twinge of sympathy.

    “He was there in his hotel, with her,” Lillian spits out. “I had never seen him look so … soft. Even on the day of our wedding, he was different. Proud and excited, but almost … rehearsed.”

    It’s easy to picture. Lex has spent Lena’s whole life acting the same exact way. He’s the life of the party, and yet, his eyes never match. There’s something distant about them, as if his inner self is trapped deep behind bars of bone and flesh. A wild animal confined without hope.

    A feeling of being untrue to one’s secret, unspoken, true inner wishes.

    It was a feeling she used to know too.

    Lillian’s voice brings Lena back to the surface. “Your father pleaded, groveled, and insisted he would do anything to save our marriage. So he sent her away and came back to his life here.”

    A heat sears in the back of Lena’s throat. Her mother was someone far too kind and worthy to be ‘sent away’ by these people. But she holds her tongue.

    “A few years later, after everything had been dealt with, your mother passed away. You were to be put into foster care, so Lionel brought you home instead. Brought you into my home.”

    Lillian’s voice cracks ever so subtly.

    “He was never the same after that.”

    Lena’s reminded of two men with the same face, one gentle and patient as he inspects a wound, and the other in a rage, his cheeks scarlet and his lips wet from whiskey and spittle.

    “The guilt ate at him constantly,” Lillian says. “Lionel didn’t like me spending time with you. I tried to keep my distance, so Lionel wouldn’t associate you with his guilt. His adultery. His betrayal of our family.”

    Ouch.

    “It was all to protect you, Lena,” Lillian coaxes. “And it took everything I had. Because you, you look so much like her. It was like ripping open a wound every time I saw you, every single day of my life.”

    It’s a confirmation, really. Once Lena had found out about her true parentage, her mind had immediately begun to connect the pieces. Every critique, every insult about Lena’s body, her weight, her clothes — it was the symptoms of a festering wound, the insecurities of a woman sundered by her husband’s infidelity.

    “Father’s been dead for eight years. That would’ve been plenty of time to summon enough bravery to rebuild a relationship with your daughter, if you truly wanted one.” Lena sucks her teeth. “Who calls their own child a whore? I was just a proxy for every insult you wanted to throw at my mother … you can’t separate me from her.”

    “I … look, honey, we’re Luthors,” Lillian says. “I have made my mistakes in this life, but there is no one else in the world who understands us.”

    That’s not true, Lena thinks. The right people do.

    “We need to stick together,” Lillian says. “Regardless of blood, you’re my daughter and I love you. We should be in each other’s lives, help each other …”

    Lillian’s true plea goes unuttered, and the absence leaves the room silent enough to hold a funeral in, until Lena draws the first breath between them.

    “I feel bad for you, Mother,” Lena says. “Because I don’t know how much of what you said today is true. And I think you’ve been lying to yourself for so long that you don’t know either. You hate both my mother and yourself, so you hate me too.”

    “Lena, I love you,” Lillian insists again. “Now, I know I didn’t show it as much as others, but—”

    “—but, exactly; you didn’t show it,” Lena says. “Regardless of if that’s the truth or not, what's the point in loving someone if they don’t feel it? It only benefits you.”

    “You’re so young, you have no idea how the world works. How much it hurts,” Lillian derides. “Can you seriously expect—”

    “—to forgive you?” Lena interjects. It’s enough to stun Lillian into silence.

    “I have,” Lena continues. “I am choosing to. I will not be like you. There’s enough pain in this world that I will not continue to bear mine like a torch. I will let it heal and love myself.”

    Lena’s heart threatens to pound out of her chest, utterly invigorated in the thrill of closure.

    “That’s why I came here today. I didn’t need any questions answered, truly, you answered them long ago in how you treated me. Once I had the missing piece, everything else made sense.”

    “I’m sorry your husband cheated on you, and you didn’t leave him for it. I’m sorry you decided to project your own insecurities and shortcomings onto your children, to manipulate and bully them to find your own sense of fulfillment, ” Lena finishes. “But I will not be a player in this game any longer.”

    “Lena …”

    “I hope you can find peace one day, Lillian. It feels pretty fucking good,” Lena inhales and rises from her seat.  “Until then, our involvement in each other’s lives will be absolutely minimal. You made me feel lonely my entire life. Surely, you’ll have some manner of expertise to call upon. Goodbye.”

    “Kara.”

    Kara freezes mid-stroke, the basketball flying awkwardly out of her hand. She turns around to give Clark as innocent a look as she can muster.

    “What?” 

    “You know, I’m not sure that’s such a good idea …” Clark shakes his head at her, his hands casually in his pockets. “Lena made a point of mentioning you’re not allowed to play basketball yet—”

    “—I’m only really using my good arm!—”

    “—and because of that you might mess up your form,” Clark continues, walking closer. “The way you’re shooting changes the ball’s weight distribution and the mechanics. You’re training your right arm to move differently and not for the better.”

    “It could be my thing, you know,” Kara says. “Supergirl, the single-arm shooter.”

    “I think ‘Supergirl the incredible, well-rounded basketball player’ sounds better,” Clark retorts. “Don’t mess up your shooting mechanics just because you’re feeling impatient.”

    Clark holds a hand out to receive the ball, and Kara begrudgingly bounce-passes it his way.

    “It feels like a shame to be here,” Kara gestures around the half-court installation in Clark’s home. “And not use it. I still have no idea how you convinced Lois to let you build this.”

    “A deal that I am still paying for,” Clark sighs. “Skipping this one time won’t hurt. Getting you healthy is the most important thing.”

    “I know,” Kara sighs. “I’m just tired of it. I want to get back out there.”

    “You will,” Clark says. “But it’s not worth rushing it. In the meantime, how about we go up on the deck for a beer? I have a gift for you.”

    “Okay,” Kara concedes with a smile, “I can’t turn down a gift.”

    “Great,” Clark grins. “You grab the beers and I’ll meet you out there.”

    Clark and Lois’ house is certainly a luxury space, but it’s humble at the same time. It’s spacious and well-furnished, but has somehow maintained a hominess reminiscent of a good farmhouse. As Kara makes her way to the kitchen, she passes the trophy case — full of basketball awards and Pulitzer prizes. She’s always hoped for a similar one some day.

    The beer is where it always is. Kara goes to bang a beer cap off using the edge of the kitchen counter, but stops. 

    A few visits ago, Lois had made a very scary and memorable threat that the next El to scuff her counters with a bottle cap would pay for it with their life. The threat of a furious Lois Lane is a good enough deterrent to have Kara searching through the copious kitchen drawers instead. By the time Kara’s found a bottle opener, Clark is back, holding a black box in his hand. 

    There’s admittedly a good deal of excitement fluttering around in Kara’s stomach. She has no idea what it could be.

    Clark grins at her and uses his head to gesture towards the patio.

    It’s gorgeous outside, a sweet May day in Metropolis. The afternoon sun shines brightly off the Metropolis skyline in the distance, glinting back and forth between skyscrapers, multiplying the light. There’s a good bit of green and gray patchwork between them and downtown. Kara smiles faintly off in the direction of Luthor Manor, knowing Lena’s there now picking up a few final belongings.

    As if he can read her mind, Clark asks, “How’s Lena doing?”

    Kara sucks her lips inward. “She’s doing okay. She hated all the attention recently but now that it’s died down, things are better. She handles it all really well.”

    “I’m sorry she had to go through that,” Clark says.

    “Yeah,” Kara sympathizes. “But Alex and I are trying our best to make sure she feels supported and as peaceful as possible.”

    “Good, I’m glad to hear it.” A guilty look settles over Clark’s face. “I haven’t heard anything from Lex. He’s off …”

    Clark waves his hand in uncertainty.

    “I don’t think Lena’s talked to him,” Kara says. “He knew and didn’t tell her. She’s very hurt.”

    “Ah,” Clark sighs. “He doesn’t often choose the right decision … I’m sorry for Lena.”

    “Me too.” 

    Clark and Kara settle into two of the chairs on the patio, facing out over the city. He sets the mysterious black box on the arm of his chair. Now that it’s in sight, Kara’s overly aware of its presence, but tries not to look at it too much, not wanting to seem impolite.

    “Your beer,” Kara says, handing the item in question to Clark.

    “Thanks,” he says, shifting around the chair with a classic old-man groan. “Urgh.”

    “Sounding very youthful, Kal,” Kara teases.

    “Just wait until it’s your turn,” Clark responds, taking a sip of his beer.

    “Yeah, yeah,” Kara rolls her eyes. “You’ll probably be at the retirement home by then, right?”

    “Don’t tempt me with a good time,” Clark says. “You know I love a good early-bird special.”

    “Have you thought about it at all?” Kara asks. “Retiring?”

    “Oh sure,” Clark says. “Here and there. Mostly when Jon refuses to sleep, really. But he’s getting older now and I think I’ve still got a good decade or so in me.”

    “Think you’ll make it to forty?”

    “That would be nice,” Clark agrees. “I’d love for Jon to remember watching me play.”

    “I’m sure he will,” Kara says. “Besides, he’ll have plenty of years of watching me play. It’s important for kids to see talented players, you know?”

    Clark scoffs. “Ouch. That cuts deep.” 

    They share a sweet laugh, gently replaced by beer in time.

    “Kal, do you think I did the right thing?” Kara asks. “With the article about my parents?”

    Clark meets her eyes, a reflection of honest blue steel. “This is a hard career, Kara. There are many distractions and conflicts that come with it. You’ll have to make hard decisions and figure out what you really want and who you want to be. It takes a great deal of strength to be vulnerable and grow as a person. That article showed the type of person you are. So yes, I do.”

    Kara feels his reassurance settle like a blanket over her shoulders. “Thanks, Kal.”

    “Your parents would be incredibly proud of you, Kara,” Clark states. “I … I think I owe you an apology.”

    “For what?”

    “For not being there for you more,” Clark says. “After you lost your parents and all.”

    “It’s okay, Kal. I understand why you made the choices you did,” Kara says. “I probably would’ve made the same ones, now that I’m where you were. The Danvers were what I needed at the time. I needed structure and support, even if I would’ve rather traveled all over with you, going from basketball game to basketball game. What kid wouldn’t?”

    “But I was your family, and I feel like I left you,” Clark admits. “You had already lost so much.”

    “I don’t resent you for it, Kal,” Kara says. “You’ve done what you could, and you’re here for me now. That’s what matters.”

    “Being a father is incredible,” Clark tells her. “Jon … I love him so much. I want the best for him. And it’s hard, it’s very difficult at times. I have to try every moment of every day. But it’s worth it. To me, he’s this symbol of hope. That there will be a better world tomorrow.”

    “I know what you mean,” Kara agrees. “It’s nice to see our family grow. That it’s not just us out here anymore.”

    “He’s an El. Jonathan El Kent,” Clark echoes the name off his son’s birth certificate. “I had something made for him.”

    Kara turns to look at her cousin with curiosity. “What?”

    Clark pulls out the golden pendant — the one they both wear — from around his neck. “I wanted to give him this, but I couldn’t part with it. It’s all I have of my biological parents, you know. It’s selfish of me … but it feels like I need to keep this to be able to remember them.”

    “I understand,” Kara murmurs in support. “It’s okay to be selfish with this, Kal.”

    “I still wanted Jon to have one. It’s his family too. So I hired a jeweler to make a new necklace,” Clark explains. “I thought that would be best. And in case Lois and I have another—“

    “Another kid?” Kara gives him a teasing smile. “Are you waging a war on sleep now? Because I think you’ll win.”

    “No, but thank you for that,” Clark retorts. “But yes, another kid. Potentially. Down the line. In a few years.”

    “You don’t sound nervous about it at all.”

    Clark gives her a faux unimpressed look, then continues. 

    “I don’t want our dads’ necklaces to be a birthright or anything,” Clark explains. “It should be equal. Every El should have one.”

    Kara nods her earnest agreement.

    “Back when Lois and I found out she was pregnant, I commissioned a jeweler, John Henry Irons, to make a new necklace, ” Clark continues. “He’s been a good friend. He made one for Jon and one for Lois.“

    “One for Lois? I haven’t seen her wearing anything,” Kara notes.

    “I haven’t given her it yet,” Clark says. “I have both of their necklaces upstairs. I wanted to talk to you before I told her about it. You’re the only other person in the world who knows how much these necklaces mean, and I wanted to ask for your blessing before I put any more into the world.”

    A warm, pleasant sensation fills Kara’s chest.

    “I love Lois and I love Jon, Kal. You should give them the necklaces as soon as you can.” Kara gives him a soft smile. “They’re my family too.”

    “Thank you, Kara,” Clark smiles in relief. “You’re okay if there’s more of our necklaces, then?”

    “Of course,” Kara says. “My dad would be thrilled that the ‘House of El’ is growing.”

    Clark chuckles. “I always liked that he called us that. It has a nice sound to it.”

    “Yeah it does,” Kara agrees. She glances down at the black box Clark had brought out. “So does that have anything to do with this conversation?”

    “It does,” Clark admits, with the bashful look of a man that’s just been read like a book page. He leans forward and hands the box to her. The box itself is gorgeous, with a sleek velvet texture and decent heft to it.  

    “Open it.”

    Kara lifts the lid to expose an object of pure gold, glittering under the Metropolis sun. It's a golden crest with an S in the middle; she knows the shape better than the back of her hand. 

    A perfect replica of the one around her neck.

    “The pendant is a little smaller than the ones we wear, and the chain a little shorter,” Clark explains. “But the rest is perfectly identical.”

    It looks perfect and Kara tells him just that. “This is for me?” she asks, a bit confused as to why she needs another necklace when she still has her dad’s.

    “Well …” Clark fidgets a bit in his chair. “That part is up to you.”

    “What do you mean?”

    “I don’t want you to feel pressured or anything, but I wanted you to have one for when you meet your Lois,” Clark explains. “ … or your Lena.”

    Oh.

    “Eliza’s known for a bit that I had more necklaces made; I had originally asked her if she thought you would be okay with me making more,” Clark explains. “When you went to the hospital after the finals, Eliza noticed Lena was wearing your necklace.”

    Busted.

    “She also mentioned that Lena was trying to hide it, which made me wonder if you felt that you two had to hide it because of me,” Clark says. “I want you to know I’m okay with however you want that necklace to be worn. I can see that Lena means so much to you. But I also don’t want you to give up a part of yourself for someone you love; it’s about building together. 

    Kara nods along in understanding.

    Clark gestures at the new necklace in Kara’s hand. “If you want to wear your necklace, but also want to have one for Lena.”

    “Kal, this is …”

    Clark raises a hand. “Now let me be perfectly clear so Eliza doesn’t kill me, I’m not saying you should go around giving this away or making any huge life commitments,” Clark urges. “But I think you should have the option — when you’re ready — to feel like you can grow our family too.”

    It takes Kara a minute to find the words, any words, as she rubs her thumb along the edges of the new pendant. It’s refreshingly cool to the touch.

    “I … thank you, Kal,” she musters up. “This means … so much to me. It’s beautiful.”

    Clark gives her a knowing smile.

    “I promise I won’t rush or lose or waste this or anything,” Kara promises. “I’ll wait until it’s right.”

    “I trust you, Kara,” Clark says. “You’re figuring life out, and you’re doing a great job.”

    “Thanks.”

    “Irons still has the template and mold,” Clark tells her. “If you decide you want to grow your side of the family any further than a life partner, we can make more.”

    Kara gives a nervous chuckle. “I think we’re a little ways out from that decision—”

    “—I agree—” Clark says firmly, in the way only an older brother can.

    “—but thank you for the sentiment. Though, I guess it's good he still has the mold for yours’ and Lois’ next kid, huh?”

    “Stop,” Clark shakes his head. “You’re causing trouble.”

    Kara grins at him, gripping the box in her hand. “Always.”

    With no small amount of spite, Lena commandeers Lex’s courtside tickets to the next Meteors game, the night before she and Kara return to National City. Jess seems more than happy to assist.

    It’s a middle-finger to her brother, to take Lex’s favored possessions and fill them with his favorite people, without him, and it settles in Lena’s stomach as more than satisfactory. 

    Lena sits on Kara’s right side. Lois sits on Kara’s other side, her infant son Jon on her lap. The fourth seat — the one that would be Lex’s in a different universe — is reserved by a diaper bag.

    It’s an amusing sight for her spiteful soul.

    She’s not the only one amused with the evening. Kara keeps leaning over to whisper an unexpected combo of sweet nothings and basketball explanations in Lena’s ear, looking like she’s found heaven on earth.

    “And what has you so happy?” Lena teases.

    Kara grins. “What doesn’t!” Her hand toys with something in her pocket.

    It should be impossible, really, the way Kara so naturally shines like a sun.

    Speaking of sons, it’s striking how much Jon resembles his father. He’s still nothing but a baby, but with a distinct head of thick dark hair and bright blue eyes. He’s even been dressed in a royal blue onesie, red earmuffs, and a bright red bib, matching the accent colors of his father’s jersey.

    “Isn’t he adorable?” Kara gently nudges Lena’s side, sprawling an arm around the back of Lena’s chair.

    Lena lets out a wobbly smile. “Mhm.”

    “Yeah, it runs in the family,” Kara lets out a deep sigh, rolling her head back to look up at Lena with mischief in her eyes. “All the El’s. We’re all utterly adorable.”

    “And so humble about it,” Lena shakes her head, looking down at her girlfriend.

    Kara’s head shoots back upright. “Well, no one’s perfect, but someone has to come close.”

    “Which is why Clark married me,” Lois joins in, leaning over towards them. “It was as close as he could get."

    A glint catches Lena's eye. There's a gold necklace dangling from her neck. It looks just the same as Kara's and Clark's. Lena briefly wonders if it's Clark's, but Kara had told her earlier than he plays with his stuffed in a sock, similar to hers tucked in her shooting sleeve. So then Lois' makes three.

    It's an interesting physical manifestation that makes Lena realize Clark sees his partner as just that — equal in all.

    Kara makes a mock pout at Lois, but whatever response the former had lined up is cut off by the sound of the crowd roaring with displeasure.

    Kara looks up at the scoreboard. “Oh, shoot,” she says. “They’re catching up.”

    The game is now tied, 45-45, with only a few minutes left before halftime.

    “Let’s go, Meteors!” Lois cheers.

    “Come on, Kal,” Kara whispers to herself. “Oh, that’s a foul! That’s a foul!”

    Lena stays silent, content to observe her surroundings. 

    It’s certainly different being at a game with Kara’s family than with Lex. Kara takes the time to explain plays and fouls, whereas Lex would always be far too engrossed to realize the minutiae of the game were often lost on his guests. Disruption was usually met with his disdain. Meanwhile Lois and Kara cheer like no one’s ever told them to be quiet. It feels to Lena like they’re more than just watchers — they’re a part of the game too.

    The score remains painfully close during the second half as well, and Kara quickly tangles into a ball of nerves, one leg shaking constantly. She looks ready to dart onto the court personally.

    “Kara, if you’re going to keep bouncing your leg like that, I’m going to put you to work,” Lois tells her, swiftly plopping Jon into her lap.

    “Sure, Lois,” Kara just laughs and holds him steady with one of her big hands sprawled across his chest. Jon leans forward into this delightful new motion, mouth agape as he looks out at the court, not understanding any of it, but unperturbed all the same.

    They look so natural together, mirror images of each other’s joy under the bright white lights of the arena. Everything is clearly visible to Lena.

    “Ooh, Jon!” Kara cooes. “Look! Your dad just dunked!”

    “Dada,” Jon babbles, as if replying to her.

    “Yeah! Your dad is Superman,” Kara tells him, very matter-of-fact. “He’s a superstar. And if you want it, maybe someday you will be too.”

    “Oh, no,” Lois groans. “No, no, by the time Clark retires, I’ll have seen enough basketball games to tide me over for the rest of my life and then some. And I definitely won’t need any more decades of basketball after your turn.”

    “There’s no such thing as too much basketball, Lois,” Kara pouts. “How can you say that?”

    There’s a brief pang in Lena’s chest; Kara and Lex really do have their kindred moments, but Lena accepts it as the growing pain it is and lets it fade.

    “With any luck, Jon will follow in his momma’s footsteps,” Lois says, “I could read his articles over my morning coffee and get to bed at a reasonable hour.”

    Though Lena doesn’t say anything, she silently hopes for the young Kent’s future to be one of his own design. 

    Hopefully, you’ll be who you want to be, Jon, Lena wishes for him. That no one successfully convinces you that you have to be something else.

    “Well, maybe he’ll be something different entirely,” Kara says, pulling Jon up with two hands towards her face. Faint relief washes through Lena’s bones. “And that’s okay. The fun part is figuring out what makes you happy, buddy.”

    Jon lets out some unintelligible gurgle in response, then spits up on himself.

    “O-kay,” Kara grimaces, handing him right back to Lois. “Back to Mom.”

    Lois shoots Kara a glare, but an understanding one at that. “Can’t handle a little spit-up? And just when I was starting to think you were all grown up.”

    “I’m fairly certain that’s impossible,” Lena teases.

    “Oh no, never!” Kara laughs. “And I get my fill of cleaning up throw up back at NCU, thank you very much.”

    Lois sighs. “Oh, yes, I remember those days. I still can’t have Franzia. Lena? What’s yours?”

    “Tequila,” Lena says. “Never again.”

    Kara laughs. “Mine’s Fireball. Alex went through quite the phase. No one was safe.”

    The roar of the crowd pulls Lena’s focus towards the court.

    Clark is hanging off the rim, all rippling muscles and pure power. The jumbotron above him replays a spectacular dunk over one of their opponents. Lena wouldn’t admit it out loud, but it’s not really her cup of tea. There’s something far more mesmerizing about the grace and finesse of Kara’s three-point shots that she prefers to these shows of brute force.

    “So, Lena,” Lois pulls Lena out of her thoughts. “You’ve heard the story of how Clark and I met; now it’s my turn. How did you and Kara end up together?”

    Heat rushes to Lena’s face. Kara squirms a little in her chair. Both of their minds race into overdrive to find a PG-rated version.

    “Oh, it's a long story, Lois,” Kara says. “It’s boring.”

    Lois Lane is not so easily derailed.

    “I doubt that,” she states. “We still have a whole other quarter to go.”

    “Well …” Lena buys herself as much precious time as she can get. “We’ve actually had a few classes together over the years.”

    “You met in class?” Lois’ eyebrows raise. “Are you sure it was Kara? I was under the impression this one’s spent more of her college career in the gym than in a classroom.” 

    She pokes Kara’s shoulder. Kara scrunches up her face in protest. “I actually do like going to class!”

    “Um, no,” Lena admits with as much grace as she can. Her face feels like it’s on fire. “We knew each other for a while but we weren’t really friends. But then this past fall, we ran into each other at a bar. We ended up … getting to know each other better.”

    Smooth, Luthor.  Lena thinks. That’s not obvious at all.

    “Getting to know each other, huh?” Lois gives her a wry smile. “Sounds just like my third date with Clark.”

    Kara seems to pointedly ignore Lois’ comment.

    “The year went on and we started to learn more about each other as people,” Lena explains. “We realized that we’re really good together.”

    “And here we are,” Kara says, her voice so casually pleased. “All just because of one night at Al’s. It was a lucky coincidence we ran into each other that night.” 

    “Oh, I don’t believe in coincidences,” Lena says. “Everything can be explained.”

    Kara turns to her, a curious look on her face. “You don’t?”

    “No.” 

    “Well, we’ll have to call it something else,” Kara gives her a soft smile. “Fate, then.”

    In that moment, it all falls away for Lena. No basketball game, no crowd, no photographers, no family drama — not even Lois and Jon register. It’s just her and Kara and the lights.

    Suddenly, Lena realizes there is truly nowhere else she’d rather be than here. She kisses Kara.

    It feels like love.

    “What was that for?” Kara chuckles after they pull away, unable to tear her eyes away from Lena’s. “Don’t tell me you really love basketball now?”

    “No,” Lena states, as simple as stone. “No, not basketball.”

    Kara grins, impossibly brighter than before. “I can’t imagine what, then.” 

    Her words are followed by another kiss, initiated by the blonde this time, as the crowd roars behind them — certainly not, but as if — on cue.

    Lena gives her a sly smile. “And what was that for?”

    Kara laughs from somewhere deep in her chest. “I just wanted to.”

    It’s the most peaceful departure from Metropolis that Lena could ask for.

    (And well, if Lena can also perfectly picture an expression of utter displeasure on Lillian’s face, when she inevitably sees a well-circulated photo of Lena with Kara at the game — well then, that’s truly just a bonus.)

    After the game ends, Clark heads straight over to join his family. It’s striking how wet his jersey is, almost soaked through, but the ensemble of black, blue, and red still matches the replica jerseys worn by everyone else in their party. Even Lena is wearing one.

    Lois slides an arm around Clark’s waist without hesitation, smiling up at the man’s glistening face. In the chaos of the game ending, Lois had placed Jon into Lena’s hands — who is more than a bit relieved to hand Jon over to Clark.

    “So, what did we think of the game?” Clark asks. He then hoists his son up, beaming at him.

    “It was honestly the best Meteors game I’ve been to,” Lena answers. It’s the truth.

    “Mine too.” Kara sets a steady hand on the small of Lena’s back. 

    “Excellent,” Clark exhales, his breathing still more rapid than at rest. He then nods at Kara. “I’ve got to enjoy my last few years of being the best Super on the court.”

    As steel blue eyes meet each other, it’s hard to say which Super looks more proud of the other.

    They’re such a family.

    And it’s not until later when Lena sees a photo from that night, of all of them huddled up together in matching jerseys, that she realizes they are a family — and she’s a part of it.

    Kara knows exactly how it happens.

    She and Lena arrive back in National City — to the latter’s great relief — the day before graduation. Graduation Day is utter chaos. The ceremony itself is boring as shit, to the point Kara contemplates trying to skip hers next year, but there’s no way Eliza will go for that, so Kara abandons that brief, blissful daydream. Afterwards is when things get chaotic. 

    The rest of the day flies by in a whirl of people and pictures and activities. Alex, clad from head to toe in her regalia, drags them all over the city, determined to get the most out of her last day of college. Ever the dutiful sister, Kara goes along with it all.  On the other hand, Lena makes her escape after lunch, followed by Eliza, who bows out after dinner. Alex mercifully allows Kara a few moments to change before the nighttime festivities begin.

    It’s basically a non-stop party from the moment they get to Al’s.

    It’s a full house tonight. The bar is alive with the sound of loud music, louder conversation, and even louder cheering. There’s still enough room to move around — just enough. Elation and celebration bubbles through the warm air.

    Kara sits in their usual booth with Lucy, the latter facing the door.

    “Uh oh, Kara,” Lucy spots something behind Kara’s head and smirks. “Your favorite person just walked in.”

    There, standing in the entryway of Al’s, with Jack and Andrea at her sides, is none other but Lena fucking Luthor, of course.

    Lena’s in a gorgeous, tight emerald dress that Kara knows. She knows how it clings to Lena’s every curve. How smooth it feels under Kara’s fingers. How it looks crumpled on the floor.

    “Sorry,” Lena says, as her group reaches the table. “I couldn’t decide what to wear.”

    Kara allows herself another moment to drool over how incredibly stunning her girlfriend is before her brain snaps back into place.

    “No apology needed,” Kara greets her, wrapping an arm around Lena’s waist. “You look incredible. Beautiful.”

    “Hey Danvers, Lena isn’t the only one here with a praise kink,” Jack quips. “How do I look?”

    “Very handsome,” Kara laughs. “Hi, Jack. Hi, Andrea.” 

    Wanting them to feel as welcome as possible, Kara promptly smothers them in a big bear hug. 

    “I’m so glad you guys were still around,” Kara says. “Come meet everyone! … Again, I guess.”

    Kara and Lena begin to take them through all the introductions, but everyone here already knows each other anyway, so they abandon ship about halfway through. Not long after, Alex comes barreling up to Kara and Lena.

    "About fucking time!” Alex throws a jovial arm over Lena’s shoulders. “We’ve been waiting for you. It’s not a party without you.”

    “Congratulations, Alex,” Lena smiles. “Have you had tonight’s drink yet?”

    “Not yet,” Alex replies, chugging down her water. “I’m still so fucking dehydrated from this morning, oh my god.”

    “Excellent,” Lena smirks and lifts her chin. “I’m about to go get myself a glass of the best scotch that Al has. Would you like one too? A little graduation present?”

    “The fancy coffee maker was plenty,” Alex gives Lena a grateful look. “But … it would be rude to decline, right?”

    “Very,” Lena teases. “Come on. Everything goes on my tab for the rest of the night.”

    Mike, the lovable mooch that he is, seems to materialize out of thin air next to Lena. “Did I just hear you’re buying?”

    “You’re surprisingly coherent for this time of night.” Alex raises her eyebrows at him.

    “I have my priorities straight,” Mike says, then looks at Lena expectantly.

    “Yes,” Lena nods.  

    Mike turns to Winn and James behind him and pumps his fists into the air excitedly. “Free Jagerb-o-o-o-ombs!” he shouts.

    “Be right back, darling,” Lena promises. She’s then promptly pulled away towards the bar.

    Kara just laughs and leans back against a corner of the wall, sipping at her beer, beyond content to soak in the sight of her girlfriend and her sister clinking their drinks together, while the boys drag Jack and Andrea into a round of Jagerbombs. Her heart seems to thrum along in unison with the bass of the music.

    Kara’s been to Al’s a hundred times, but never did she think this is how a night here would go. 

    Her friends and Lena’s friends pass the night away together, drinking and dancing like maniacs. It’s incredible, really, how much their lives have changed over the course of a year.

    From halfway across the room, Lena’s eyes find hers, flitting south down Kara’s body.

    Kara, while making eye contact with Lena the entire time, grins and unbuttons the next button of her shirt. And another. She can’t help herself. 

    Lena rolls her eyes and throws back the shot in her hand.

    Kara loses sight of her for a moment as people shift around the bar. Then — she’s right there.

    “Danvers,” Lena smirks, sauntering up to Kara. One of Lena’s hands slides up Kara’s neck and pulls her into a deep kiss. Kara can feel Lena’s tongue between her teeth, pulling at her own tongue.

    When they come up for air, Kara grins into Lena’s lips. 

    “Luthor,” Kara replies. She’s sure to have Lena’s bright red lipstick smeared across her face now, but she really couldn’t care less.

    “You look oddly deep in thought for someone who’s drinking cheap beer at a seedy dive bar at midnight,” Lena remarks.

    “Yeah,” Kara exhales, her mouth pulling upwards into a smile. “I just … I’m just soaking it all in.”

    “Admiring the timeless decor of a bar that’s never once been renovated since it opened, decades ago?” Lena asks, voice laden with sarcasm.

    “That part not so much,” Kara agrees. She gestures out at the main room of the bar, more full of life than she’s ever seen before.

    “Everything’s going to change,” Kara says. “It’ll never be like this again.”

    Lena’s face immediately drops into a look of concern. “What are you worried about, darling?”

    “I’m not,” Kara reassures. “I’m nervous, and excited, and a little scared. Change is always a bit scary. But I’m more excited than scared. I think we have such exciting things to do ahead.”

    “We do,” Lena promises.

    “I never thought this would be my life,” Kara says. “There's still a part of me that’s the scared, awkward, lonely kid who basically crash-landed in Midvale. Then I came here. People suddenly gave me so much attention and adoration because of basketball.  I was only ever alone when I wanted to be. I started to make friends, to fit in. I found a really good group of people here.”

    Lena rubs reassuringly at Kara’s collarbone.

    “I never expected this. I never expected to find you, Lena,” Kara admits. “You understand me. You help make me a better person.”

    “Hardly,” Lena says. “You’ve been an incredible person since as long as I’ve known you. I just offer you the same compassion and consideration you show everyone else.”

    “And way more. We’re all like a little family,” Kara finishes. “And it’s going to change now. I guess I … I just hope that I’ll find it again.”

    “You will. It might look a little different, but you will. We’ll figure it out,” Lena offers. “I'm not going anywhere, Danvers. We’re stronger together, right?”

    Kara looks at Lena, and as far as she’s concerned, there’s only one sun in the solar system, and she’s right here, in a beloved dive bar of National City.

    “Stronger together,” Kara vows.

    They’re drunk and in love and they can’t help but make out a little. Lena fills Kara’s every sense, the heat of her body, the sleek fabric of her dress, the smell of expensive shampoo and perfume, the faint taste of scotch in her mouth.

    Kara can’t get enough of her.

    Once they pull away for air, Lena teases, “So, you really can’t stand buttons, can you?”

    She slides two of her fingers down the inside Kara’s shirt, her knuckles scraping against Kara’s abs. Kara flexes them on instinct.

    “I don’t really see a need for them,” Kara shrugs, all-too-innocent. “Not around you.”

    “Admittedly, it would be a bummer if I couldn’t do this,” Lena bites her lip and runs her fingers up Kara’s chest until they hit fabric again.

    “You have a very high opinion of me,” Kara jokes.

    Lena cocks her chin out at Kara. “I have excellent taste in partners.”

    “Is that right?” Kara says, her voice heavy with sex. She runs her hand up the side of Lena’s hip to the small of her back. “You feel so warm.”

    “You’ve been eye-fucking me ever since I got here,” Lena says. “How’s a girl supposed to keep her cool?” 

    “Maybe you shouldn’t.”

    “Is that so?” Lena looks about ready to devour her. 

    “I want you,” Kara exhales. “So bad.”

    Lena gives Kara a wicked smile, framed in bright red. “I love it when we agree on things, darling.”

    “I can call us a ride-share,” Kara says, hand already fishing in her back pocket for her phone. “Alex will be pissed if we disappear but I’m really, really okay with that right now.”

    “No,” Lena shakes her head. “We can’t leave. I made plans with everyone; we’re all going to Bob’s Diner after last call. We need to stay here.”

    “Oh,” Kara says, mind vaulting through the mental calculus. She is hungry. Some bacon and french toast would certainly be a welcome addition to the night, and if Lena voluntarily organized plans with everyone, then they have to go. 

    “So then …?” Kara gives Lena a quizzical look.

    Lena’s eyes wander not-so-innocently over to the bathroom door. 

    “There’s no line, unexplainably,” Lena says. “It could be fate.”

    “No!” Kara gasps. “Did you just … are we … who are you?”

    “Don’t give me enough time to change my mind,” Lena states, already pulling at Kara’s belt buckle.

    “Are you sure you want this?” Kara checks, simultaneously running her hands up Lena’s back, searching for the zipper.

    “Yes,” Lena says, breath hot against Kara’s neck. “I want you.”

    “I want you too,” Kara declares. 

    Her back hits the bathroom door open with a ‘thwack’, and that’s the quietest sound the bathroom walls hear for a while. What comes next is a whirlwind like no other. Something Kara never, ever, ever would have thought would happen.

    But it’s too fitting for them not to.

    So they do.
